name: Thule Inuit expansion across the Arctic
story: Around 1200 CE, Thule whalers expanded east from Alaska through the Canadian Arctic and into Greenland. Late Dorset communities persisted in parts of the central and eastern Canadian Arctic and northwest Greenland during that broad expansion; radiocarbon evidence places Late Dorset occupation after 1300 in southeastern Victoria Island, with Thule settlement in adjacent regions. The regional succession is clear, but direct contact, violence, and a Thule-caused expulsion remain unproved. This northern Dorset–Thule history is separate from the southwest Greenland farm districts settled by the Norse around 985, where no reviewed evidence places a resident Late Dorset community at landnám.
displaced: Late Dorset people (Tuniit)
settlers: Thule Inuit (ancestral Inuit), from northern Alaska and the Bering Strait
note: An expansion case, not a claim that Inuit are foreign colonizers in any modern legal sense. Thule people are the direct ancestors of today's Inuit. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

targets.name: Central and eastern Canadian Arctic — regional succession and documented late Dorset persistence
Northwest Greenland — Late Dorset and later Thule occupation

contested: Late Dorset and Thule occupation overlapped or were adjacent in parts of the central/eastern Canadian Arctic and northwest Greenland. That does not by itself establish face-to-face contact or direct displacement. The map does not place Late Dorset residents in the southwest Norse settlement districts in 985.

name: Teutonic conquest & colonization of Prussia
story: In 1226 the Golden Bull of Rimini, an imperial charter from Frederick II, handed the Teutonic Order a crusade against the pagan Old Prussians. Fifty years of war broke them, and the Great Prussian Uprising of 1260–74 was the last serious resistance. Behind the knights came castles, chartered towns under Kulm law, and German-speaking farmers, and the Baltic-speaking Prūsai were killed, subjected, Christianized and slowly absorbed until their language died out entirely by the eighteenth century.
displaced: Old Prussians, the Prūsai (Pomesanians, Sambians, Nadruvians and others)
settlers: German-speaking colonists of the Holy Roman Empire
the Teutonic Order
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Christian colonization of Valencia
story: When James I of Aragon took Valencia in 1238, scribes wrote the colonization down in the Llibre del Repartiment, house by house and field by field, the property of a Muslim kingdom handed to Christian settlers from Catalonia and Aragon. The newcomers ruled as a minority over a Mudéjar majority for generations, colonial settlement without immediate demographic replacement. Robert Burns called it exactly that, medieval colonialism, the exploitation of a subject population through tax and lordship.
displaced: Muslim Valencians (Mudéjars)
later Moriscos
settlers: Christian settlers from Catalonia and Aragon
note: A localized medieval case. The later forced conversions and the 1609 expulsion of the Moriscos belong to a longer history not shown here as one continuous phase. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

story: Over seven centuries the Vietnamese state moved south, absorbing the Cham and Khmer lands along the coast. The hinge was 1471, when Lê Thánh Tông stormed the Cham capital Vijaya. Vietnamese annals claim 60,000 killed and 30,000 taken, an event George Dutton frames as the genocide of Champa. Nguyễn lords then colonized the Khmer Mekong delta, including Prey Nokor, the future Saigon, before Minh Mạng annexed the last Cham principality in 1832.

contested: Worldwide audit correction: A 763-year umbrella conflates conquest of Cham polities, Vietnamese settler movement, incorporation of the Mekong delta, and later Nguyễn state colonization; each phase affected different peoples and places.

name: Inca resettlement system (mitma)
story: The Inca colonized from within. From Pachacuti's reign the state uprooted whole communities, the mitmaqkuna, and transplanted them across Tawantinsuyu. Loyal colonists were planted among the newly conquered, rebels scattered far from home, farmers moved to open the maize estates of the Cochabamba valley. Cañari and Chachapoya potters carried Cusco techniques a thousand kilometres north, a physical trace of forced migration. The Spanish conquest shattered the system, and the displaced tried to walk home.
contested: Applying “settler colonialism” to an Indigenous Andean empire is debated, and mitma is more often described as imperial resettlement. It is here as an internal-colonization case.

story: England colonized Ireland by planting it. The policy opened under Mary I with Laois–Offaly in 1556, ran through Munster after the Desmond wars, and reached its scale in Ulster from 1609, where six escheated counties were parcelled to English and Scottish settlers. By 1641 perhaps 100,000 British migrants had arrived, tens of thousands of them Lowland Scots. Catholic-held land fell from around three-fifths of the island to a seventh by 1703 as war and confiscation did their work.

story: After Kazan fell in 1552 the Bashkirs kept their patrimonial land rights on paper, and lost them in practice. Forts at Ufa and Orenburg anchored colonization, and revolt after revolt was crushed, in 1662, 1704, 1735–40, and again under Salawat Yulayev in the Pugachev rising. Between 1869 and 1878 alone the state alienated nearly a million desiatinas of Bashkir land through forced sales. Edyta Bojanowska's study shows even Tolstoy buying Bashkir steppe cheap while its nomads were pushed off.

name: Circassia
story: The end of the Russo-Circassian war in 1864 was also the emptying of a homeland. When the last resistance broke at Qbaada above Sochi, Russia expelled the Adyghe wholesale to the Ottoman Empire. Walter Richmond estimates at least 600,000 dead of massacre, starvation and exposure, roughly three-quarters of the Circassian people. The survivors scattered to Turkey, Jordan and Syria, and Cossack colonists settled the cleared coast.

story: Russian protection over the Kazakh khans, sworn in 1731, hardened into land seizure. Roughly 1.5 million settlers from European Russia and Ukraine took the pasture in the late-tsarist colonization surge, and the khanates were abolished outright. Then Soviet collectivization brought famine: Sarah Cameron finds about 1.5 million dead in 1930–33, some 1.3 million of them Kazakhs, proportionally the worst toll of any Soviet nationality. It left Kazakhs a minority in their own republic for decades.

story: The treaties of Aigun and Peking, 1858–60, handed Russia the Amur and Ussuri from a weakened Qing, and the Cossack hosts moved onto the river line. Subsidized steamship passage from Odesa filled it fast. By 1913 about 250,000 peasants had arrived, three-quarters of them Ukrainian, which gave the settlement belt its name, Zelenyi Klyn, the Green Wedge. The Nanai, Udege, Nivkh and Orochi became small minorities, and in 1937 the Soviet state deported 172,000 Koreans to Central Asia to finish reordering the coast.

story: Four states enclosed the Sámi north. Swedish colonization pushed in from the 1630s with silver mining at Nasafjäll, which conscripted Sámi to haul ore by reindeer, and a 1673 proclamation then invited farmers onto Sámi taxed lands. Norway's Norwegianization ran from 1851 to the 1980s, banning the language in schools, while Sweden's nomad-school policy kept reindeer-herding Sámi in separate, inferior classrooms. Åsa Össbo reads the mining, the hydropower dams and today's wind farms as one long industrial colonialism.

contested: Worldwide audit correction: Four states used different settlement, taxation, schooling, mining, border-closure, and land policies over several centuries; a single cross-border case erases those differences.

story: Han Taiwan grew from a few thousand to a few million in two centuries. Hoklo migrants from Fujian and Hakka from Guangdong crossed the strait under the Dutch, the Zheng regime and then the Qing, and a Qing count in 1811 recorded 1.9 million people, overwhelmingly Han. The plains Austronesian peoples, the Siraya, Babuza and others, lost their land through Qing leasing and mortgage law and were absorbed, while the mountain nations held out until Japanese campaigns after 1895.

story: The Qing did not just conquer the Zünghars. They erased them. In 1755–58 the Qianlong emperor's armies, aided by smallpox, destroyed the Oirat Mongol state of Dzungaria, and Peter Perdue and others estimate that 70–80% of the population died or fled, on the order of half a million people. Then the Qing repopulated the emptied land from 1759 with Han and Hui farmers, Manchu and Sibe bannermen, and Taranchi Uyghur cultivators. It was a deliberate colonization of a cleared frontier.

contested: Worldwide audit correction: The destruction of the Dzungar polity and population, postwar repopulation by multiple groups, and later military-agricultural colonization are causally linked but distinct events.

story: Inner Mongolia became a Han land through the plow. From about 1902 the late-Qing “New Policies” reversed the old ban and opened Mongol banner pasture to farming, pushing herders toward sedentarization and provoking the duguilang revolts. Warlords and settlers kept coming, and then the PRC drove large-scale in-migration from the 1950s through state farms and industry. Mongols, roughly a fifth of the region in 1949, fell to about 17–18% of some 24 million people, a minority in their own autonomous region.
contested: Beijing frames the region as an integral autonomous region and the migration as internal development, while the settler-colonial reading comes mainly from outside scholars such as Uradyn Bulag. Worldwide audit correction: Late-Qing cultivation policy, Republican-era migration, PRC state farms, collectivization, and post-1978 urban expansion have different institutions and local effects.

settlers: Han Chinese farmers and, later, state-organized migrants

story: The People's Liberation Army entered eastern Tibet in 1950, and the Seventeen Point Agreement formalized Chinese sovereignty in 1951. Emily Yeh's Taming Tibet shows how state development remade Lhasa and drew Han traders and workers into its economy, accelerated by the Qinghai–Tibet railway in 2006. Han remain a minority in the Tibet Autonomous Region proper, and Andrew Fischer reads the 2020 census at about 12%, but they dominate its towns and are far more numerous in the Tibetan areas of Qinghai and Sichuan.
contested: Genuinely disputed. Gerald Roche and Ju-Han Zoe Wang argue the case through settler-colonial theory, while the People's Republic rejects the frame, calling 1950–51 the peaceful liberation of Tibet and noting that Han remain a TAR minority. Worldwide audit correction: The entry must distinguish voluntary and state-facilitated migration, military-administrative control, pastoralist relocation, boarding schools, and disputed claims of demographic replacement.

story: In 1869 the Meiji state annexed Ezo, renamed it Hokkaidō, and set up a Colonization Commission that spent 20 million yen settling the island. From 1874 samurai-farmer militia colonists took Ainu land, and the population passed a million by 1901. The 1899 Former Aborigines Protection Act gave Ainu poorer farmland and forced Japanese schooling, and stood until 1997. Only in 2019 did Japan recognize the Ainu as an Indigenous people, and a survey counts about 13,000, widely thought an undercount.

name: Japanese Korea
story: Japanese settlers reached Korea from the 1876 treaty ports, three decades before annexation, and some 170,000 were already there in 1910. Jun Uchida calls them the brokers of empire. Their number neared 700,000 by the 1940s, one of the century's largest colonial settler communities, expanding on the back of a 1910–18 cadastral survey and the Oriental Development Company's landholdings. In 1945 nearly all of them were repatriated, reversing the settlement order in a single year.
displaced: Koreans (dominated and dispossessed in place)
settlers: Japanese civilian settlers (merchants, officials and farmers)
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Japanese Micronesia
story: Japan seized Germany's Micronesian islands in 1914 and ran them as the Nan'yō. Sugar drew settlers by the tens of thousands, most from Okinawa: by 1937 Japanese outnumbered Islanders across the whole mandate, about 62,000 to 50,000, and Saipan's Garapan was nearly all Japanese. In Palau, incomers were 60% of the population by 1935. Japan's 1945 defeat repatriated almost all of them, and the settler order collapsed as fast as it had risen.

story: Britain founded the Port Blair penal colony in 1858 to hold rebels of 1857, and the settlement it seeded destroyed the islanders. The Great Andamanese collapsed from several thousand at contact to 625 by 1901 and an all-time low of 19 in 1961, wrecked by measles, influenza and syphilis. After 1947 India settled Partition refugees and mainland labourers, and some 400,000 people now vastly outnumber a few hundred Great Andamanese, Onge, Jarawa and Sentinelese, whose forests a trunk road still cuts through.

story: State-backed settlement turned a Muslim island into a Christian-majority one. American authorities opened agricultural colonies in Cotabato from 1913. Around 1.2 million migrants entered in 1948–60 alone. The Moro peoples fell from roughly three-quarters of Mindanao's population at 1900 to about a quarter by 1948, and the Lumad to a small minority, their customary land redefined as public.

story: After the 1954 partition, Diem's government began resettling lowland Kinh, including northern Catholic refugees, in the highlands. name: Chittagong Hill Tracts
story: Bangladesh moved its lowlanders uphill. A covert state program from 1979 to 1984 shifted more than 400,000 Bengali settlers into the Chittagong Hill Tracts with land grants and rations, and the Bengali share of the population jumped from 12% in 1974 to nearly half by 1991. The 1962 Kaptai Dam had already drowned 40% of the best farmland and displaced 100,000 people, mostly Chakma. Counter-insurgency against the Jumma peoples brought massacres through the 1980s and 90s, and the 1997 peace accord's land promises remain largely unmet.

story: Sri Lanka colonized its own dry zone. State-aided schemes from the 1935 Land Development Ordinance moved Sinhalese peasants into districts Tamils and Muslims claimed, redrawing the electoral map, and Patrick Peebles reads the whole program as a driver of the ethnic conflict. The sharpest case is Weli Oya, carved out of Tamil-majority Manal Aru in 1984 and militarized. Tamil residents got 48-hour eviction notices, and by 2012 the area's 18 villages were 99.7% Sinhalese. The war it fed brought massacres on both sides.
contested: Scale, intent and the settler-colonial label are strongly disputed. The Weli Oya scheme is the clearest instance, the wider dry-zone program more debated. Worldwide audit correction: Gal Oya, Mahaweli, Weli Oya, and other schemes had different dates, sponsors, ethnic politics, and displacement footprints; one national label is not an event-level account.

Muslims of contested eastern districts
settlers: Sinhalese peasant colonists from the south and centre, state-sponsored
note: Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

story: Indonesia took West Papua's administration in 1963 and ratified it through the 1969 “Act of Free Choice,” a vote of 1,022 hand-picked electors. Non-Papuans were 4% of the population in 1971. By 2010, after decades of transmigration and spontaneous migration from Java and Sulawesi, settlers were a slight majority overall, and Jim Elmslie projected the Indigenous share falling below 30%. New transmigration plans floated in 2024 drew fresh Papuan protest. The highlands remain overwhelmingly Papuan. The coasts and towns do not.
contested: The settler-colonial framing is advanced by scholars such as Jim Elmslie and by Papuan advocates, while Indonesia rejects it, treating Papua as an integral province. Worldwide audit correction: Military occupation, formal transmigration, spontaneous migration, resource concessions, urban land seizure, and conflict displacement require separate dates and evidentiary claims.
displaced: Papuans (Melanesian peoples, incl. the Moi of Sorong)
settlers: Javanese and Madurese transmigrants

note: Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

story: Germany declared a protectorate in 1884 and built its only true settler colony on the land it seized. When the Herero rose in 1904 and the Nama followed, General von Trotha issued an extermination order. By 1908 roughly 65,000 Herero, four in five, and at least 10,000 Nama were dead by shooting, thirst in the Omaheke, and the camps at Shark Island. South Africa took over in 1915 and extended apartheid until independence in 1990. Germany acknowledged the genocide only in 2021.

contested: Worldwide audit correction: German conquest, the Herero and Nama genocide, settler land allocation, and South African mandate/apartheid rule were distinct regimes; ending only at independence hides the changing machinery.

name: Southern Rhodesia / Zimbabwe
story: Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company sent a Pioneer Column into Mashonaland in 1890, and war finished the conquest, the Ndebele kingdom in 1893 and the Shona and Ndebele risings of 1896–97. The 1930 Land Apportionment Act handed roughly half the colony to about 48,000 whites, under 5% of the people. Ian Smith declared independence in 1965 to preserve minority rule, and the settler population peaked near 300,000 before the liberation war ended the settler state at Zimbabwe's independence in 1980.

name: Kenya Highlands
story: Britain reserved Kenya's best land for whites and called it the White Highlands. Crown Lands ordinances from 1902 let settlers take 999-year leases, and the 1939 Highlands Order fenced roughly 7.5 million acres off from Africans, policed by a board that vetted every sale. The Maasai were moved south by “agreement” in 1904 and 1911. Over 200,000 Kikuyu lived as squatter-labourers on settler farms, and their eviction and land hunger fed the Mau Mau uprising and the emergency of 1952–60.

name: Liberia
story: A settler colony of freed slaves. The American Colonization Society planted its first settlers at Cape Mesurado in 1822, and by 1867 had sent more than 13,000 African American emigrants. The colony declared itself a republic in 1847 with a constitution written by and for the settler class. The Americo-Liberians, a few percent of the population, ruled the Indigenous majority through the True Whig Party from 1878 until Samuel Doe's 1980 coup ended their monopoly, a distinctive Black, non-metropolitan case of the same structure.

name: Argentina: Pampas & Patagonia
story: Argentina cleared its south by campaign. Law 215 of 1867 set the conquest of the Indigenous frontier as state policy, and from 1878 General Roca's Conquest of the Desert drove it home with breech-loading rifles, killing and capturing thousands of Mapuche, Ranquel and Tehuelche and interning prisoners on Martín García island. The last cacique, Sayhueque, surrendered in 1885. The conquered land, some 8.5 million hectares from one campaign's bonds, went to a few hundred owners and to the European immigrants pouring through Buenos Aires.

name: Chile: Araucanía
story: For two centuries Spain recognized Mapuche autonomy south of the Biobío, and Chile ended it by force. Colonel Saavedra's occupation of Araucanía, planned from 1861, advanced with forts and towns. The last general Mapuche uprising broke in 1881, and the re-founding of Villarrica in 1883 closed the conquest. The state then penned Mapuche communities into some 3,000 reducciones, about 500,000 hectares of their former country, and handed the rest to Chilean and European colonists, Germans and Swiss and Boers among them.

story: Uruguay built its European self-image on a massacre. On 11 April 1831, President Fructuoso Rivera's forces ambushed the Charrúa at Salsipuedes, killing about 40 and taking 300 prisoner, and four captives were shipped to Paris in 1833 and exhibited. Mass Spanish and Italian immigration then filled the country and let the state call itself a país sin indios, a land without Indians. It was never true, and Charrúa descendants organized from 1989 and now contest the story of their own extinction.
note: A qualified case. The displaced Charrúa were a small, mobile population, and Uruguay's settler majority came mostly from later European immigration rather than from replacing a large Indigenous society. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

placeGloss: The 1831 forced movement ran from the Salsipuedes capture zone toward Montevideo and other destinations. Spain and Italy belong only to the later immigration stage preserved in the dated sequence.
contested: Worldwide audit correction: The Salsipuedes campaign and subsequent removal, captivity, land privatization, and transborder Indigenous survival need their own bounded events; '1831–20th century' is not a usable chronology.

name: Mennonite Chaco, Paraguay
story: A settler colony with no metropole behind it. Paraguay's 1921 law promised Mennonites exemption from military service, oaths and state schooling, and in 1927 the first 1,743 pioneers from Canada founded Menno Colony in the Chaco, and refugees from the Soviet Union followed in 1930 and 1947. The colonies occupy Enlhet, Nivaclé and Ayoreo land, and their cooperatives now run the central Chaco's cattle-and-dairy economy while some Ayoreo-Totobiegosode still live in voluntary isolation in the shrinking forest.

story: Bolivia turned east after its 1952 revolution. The US-backed Plan Bohan had drawn the blueprint, and the 1953 agrarian reform and later governments opened colonization corridors in Santa Cruz and the Chapare, moving Andean Quechua and Aymara settlers, plus state-recruited Mennonite and Okinawan colonies, into the lowlands. Ben Nobbs-Thiessen traces how this remade Santa Cruz into an agro-industrial heartland, and the two colonization zones account for most of Bolivia's deforestation, at the expense of Guaraní, Ayoreo and Chiquitano land.

name: New Caledonia
story: France annexed New Caledonia in 1853 and settled it partly with convicts, some 22,000 transported to 1897, including 4,250 Communards. Land ceded to colonists rose from 1,000 hectares in 1860 to 230,000 by 1878, the year Grand Chief Ataï's revolt was crushed at the cost of a thousand Kanak lives. Governor Feillet then cut the Kanak reserves from 320,000 to 120,000 hectares. The Kanak, reduced from perhaps 60,000 to 27,000 by 1900, are now about 40% of the population, and three independence referendums have failed.

settlers: French convicts and free settlers (Caldoches)

story: New England missionaries arrived in 1820 and their families became Hawaiʻi's landholding, sugar-growing elite. The 1848 Māhele broke up the traditional land system and let foreigners buy in, and many makaʻāinana ended up with nothing. In 1893 a committee of planters overthrew Queen Liliʻuokalani with U.S. Marines behind them. A petition of 21,000 Kānaka Maoli, more than half those counted, defeated the annexation treaty, so Congress annexed the islands by simple resolution in 1898. The Native population had fallen from perhaps 300,000 at contact to about 40,000.
contested: The status of later Asian plantation-labour migrants is itself debated. Fujikane and Okamura's “Asian settler colonialism” frames it, and the debate is part of the record. Worldwide audit correction: Missionary-commercial settlement, the Māhele land regime, overthrow and annexation, plantation labor importation, military land taking, and post-statehood development are distinct processes.

story: Guam was colonized twice. Spain's conquest from 1668 imposed the reducción, and war and disease cut the CHamoru to about 3,500 by 1710. The United States took the island in 1898 and layered a second colonization over the first. After retaking Guam in 1944, the U.S. military seized 52,000 acres and at its peak held 63% of Guåhan, condemning most of it in 1948 at pre-war prices. Roughly 28% remains under military control, and the CHamoru are a minority on their own island, in an unincorporated territory whose residents still cannot vote for president.

name: Rapa Nui
story: Rapa Nui nearly disappeared before Chile ever raised its flag. Peruvian slavers seized over 1,400 people in 1862–63, a third to a half of the island, and the smallpox the few survivors carried home killed roughly a thousand more, dropping the population to about 100. Chile annexed the island in 1888, then leased it to a Scottish-Chilean sheep company that penned the Rapanui behind a wall at Hanga Roa until the 1960s. Only the 1966 Ley Pascua gave them citizenship and the run of their own island.
displaced: Rapanui
settlers: European ranchers (Williamson-Balfour Company)
the Chilean state, navy and mainland migrants
note: The 1862–63 slave raids and first ranching predate the 1888 annexation that opens this record. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Vanuatu / New Hebrides
story: The New Hebrides were worked over twice: labour taken out, planters moved in. Between 1863 and 1904, blackbirding carried more than 60,000 South Sea Islanders to Queensland's plantations, many of them ni-Vanuatu. French and British planters then alienated so much land that by the mid-twentieth century over a third of the islands was foreign-owned, though the ni-Vanuatu stayed the majority. At independence in 1980, the new constitution reversed a century of it in one line: all land belongs to the indigenous custom owners.
displaced: ni-Vanuatu (Indigenous Melanesian peoples)
settlers: French planters and land companies
British and Australian planters
condominium officials
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Banaba (Ocean Island)
story: An island eaten for fertilizer. Britain annexed Banaba in 1900, the year phosphate was found, and the British Phosphate Commissioners, owned by Britain, Australia and New Zealand, strip-mined about 90% of its surface, shipping more than 20 million tonnes to Antipodean farms. In December 1945 the surviving Banabans were moved 2,000 km to Rabi Island in Fiji, bought with money from their own phosphate trust. Katerina Teaiwa calls it the literal consumption of a homeland, and the deposits ran out in 1979, as Kiribati became independent.
contested: Banaba was not a conventional replacement colony. It is included because imperial annexation, phosphate extraction that destroyed most habitable land, and the coerced relocation of Banabans to Rabi formed one connected process of land destruction and displacement.
displaced: Banabans (te aomata ni Banaba), forcibly resettled to Rabi, Fiji in 1945
settlers: Imported mine labourers (Chinese and Pacific Islander) under the phosphate regime
mechanism: Extractive colonialism and forced relocation
affectedLabel: Displaced
actorLabel: Colonial / company actors
note: Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; high confidence.

name: Posen & West Prussia
story: Imperial Germany tried to colonize its own Polish provinces and mostly failed. Bismarck's 1886 law created a Royal Settlement Commission with 100 million marks to buy Polish land for German farmers, and funding eventually topped 950 million marks. But of 438,000 hectares it acquired, only a quarter came from Polish owners, most bought from Germans, and Polish land banks out-competed it. By 1918 it had settled about 22,000 German families, far short of its aim. Its most durable product was the 1908 law letting the state expropriate Polish estates outright.
displaced: Poles (Polacy)
settlers: German peasant colonist families recruited by the Settlement Commission
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Generalplan Ost
story: The most murderous settlement plan ever drafted, and only partly carried out. Under Himmler, the agronomist Konrad Meyer's office designed Generalplan Ost to expel some 31 million people, far more in later versions, beyond the Urals and settle Germans in their place across Poland, Ukraine, Belarus and the Baltics. Implementation reached the Zamość region, where from November 1942 about 100,000 Poles, including 30,000 children, were driven from 297 villages to make room for ethnic-German settlers before the war turned.

note: A genocidal settler-colonial plan with partial implementation, not a completed settler society. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; high confidence.
contested: Worldwide audit correction: The attempted plan must be separated from the actually implemented expulsions, deportations, Germanization, mass murder, and settlement experiments under Nazi occupation.

name: French Algeria
story: France invaded in 1830 and stayed 132 years, seizing land and political power while remaining a tenth of the population. The conquest itself was catastrophic, and Algeria's Muslim population fell by perhaps a third between 1830 and the 1870s through war, dispossession and famine. Europeans, the pieds-noirs, numbered about 984,000 by 1954, holding some 2.7 million hectares of the best farmland. When independence came in 1962, nearly the whole settler community left, around 650,000 in that year alone.
displaced: Muslim Algerians (Arab and Amazigh communities)
settlers: European settlers (pieds-noirs) of French, Spanish, Italian and Maltese origin
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; high confidence.

story: Italy's settlement of Libya came after an atrocity. To break Cyrenaican resistance from 1929 to 1934, Badoglio and Graziani deported the population to sixteen concentration camps. Ali Abdullatif Ahmida documents more than 60,000 deaths, and Omar al-Mukhtar was hanged before a crowd in 1931. Only then did the Fascist “demographic colonization” begin, the Ventimila, 20,000 settlers shipped in one 1938 convoy into purpose-built villages, some 110,000 Italians by 1940. The Allied conquest of 1943 ended it.
note: A qualified case. The demographic colonization was large but brief, cut off by the 1943 Allied conquest before it settled into a permanent society. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

story: When Spain withdrew in 1975, Morocco moved in. King Hassan II's Green March sent some 350,000 civilians across the border, and the territory was partitioned. Within months tens of thousands of Sahrawis had fled to refugee camps near Tindouf in Algeria, whose population is disputed, with UNHCR planning figures near 90,000 and Polisario counts far higher. Morocco later presented the UN with lists of 120,000 settlers it had moved in since 1975. The UN still lists Western Sahara as a non-self-governing territory with no administering power, and M. Padrón Hernández argues it should be read as a settler colony.
contested: There is no reliable census. The claim that settlers now outnumber Sahrawis in the territory is standard but not precisely quantifiable. Worldwide audit correction: The 1975 invasion and refugee flight, wartime wall and mine displacement, subsidized Moroccan settlement, and continuing resource and housing policy require separate representation.
displaced: Sahrawis
settlers: Moroccan settlers
note: The markers fall west of the berm, in the Moroccan-controlled zone. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

name: Northern Cyprus
story: Turkey's 1974 invasion split the island and set two populations moving. About 160,000 to 180,000 Greek Cypriots fled south and 45,000 to 60,000 Turkish Cypriots north. Then came organized settlement. A 1975 labour protocol aimed to bring some 30,000 mainland Turks to farm the emptied north, and heavy settlement continued to 1977. The eventual settler total is fiercely disputed. The 2011 census counted 295,000 residents of every kind, Turkish Cypriots and the locally born children of settlers among them, and estimates of actual mainland settlers range widely, which is why the numbers, intent and the label all remain contested.
contested: Numbers, intent and the settler-colonial classification are all strongly disputed. Scholars reject the highest settler estimates as speculative.
displaced: Greek Cypriots (displaced south)
Turkish Cypriots (moved north)
settlers: Mainland Turkish settlers
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Iraqi Kurdistan & Kirkuk
story: Baʼathist Iraq re-engineered its north by Arabization. From the mid-1970s some 250,000 Kurds and other non-Arabs were expelled from a wide belt of the north, their land and homes handed to Arab families moved up from the centre and south. The 1988 Anfal campaign under Ali Hassan al-Majid reached genocidal scale, and Human Rights Watch documents the disappearance of about 100,000 Kurds, with the chemical attack on Halabja killing roughly 5,000 in a day. The expulsions from Kirkuk continued until the regime fell in 2003.

Turkmen
Assyrians
settlers: Arab families relocated from central and southern Iraq with state land and housing
note: Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Syrian Arab Belt
story: Syria planned an Arab cordon along its Kurdish north. In 1962 a special census had stripped some 120,000 Jazira Kurds of citizenship, and the 1965 “Arab Belt” scheme then envisaged an Arabized strip 15 km deep and 280 km long on the Turkish border. In 1975 the state settled about 4,000 Arab families, farmers displaced by the Tabqa Dam, in 41 model villages built on land taken from Kurds, many of them the very people denaturalized in 1962. Assad suspended the plan in 1976 but never dismantled the villages.
displaced: Kurds of al-Hasakah / Jazira
settlers: ~4,000 Arab families displaced by the Tabqa Dam, settled 1975 in 41 model farms
note: Planning began in the 1960s. Implementation ran 1973–75 and was suspended in 1976, leaving the villages in place. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Yayoi settlement of Japan
story: Japan's islands were held for millennia by the Jomon, hunter-gatherers with their own pottery and a deep genetic signature. From around 900 BCE, wet-rice farmers known as the Yayoi crossed from the southern Korean peninsula into Kyushu and spread northeast. Cooke and colleagues read the arrival as a massive influx that absorbed rather than erased the Jomon, followed by a further continental wave in the Kofun period. Jomon ancestry survives in modern Japanese at only about ten to fifteen percent, so the cumulative turnover was large even where each step was admixture.
contested: Whether to call this replacement or absorption is genuinely open. The single Yayoi transition looks closer to an even mix, but the added Kofun influx leaves the older ancestry a small minority, so the long-run outcome is demographic dominance by newcomers.
displaced: Jomon hunter-gatherers
settlers: Yayoi wet-rice farmers from the Korean peninsula
later Kofun-era continental migrants
note: An expansion case read from ancient DNA, and a strong non-European case of farming-driven population turnover. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Anglo-Saxon settlement of Britain
story: As Roman Britain fell apart, people from the North Sea coast, Jutland, Lower Saxony and Frisia, crossed into its eastern lowlands. The old question was whether a few warlords imposed a language on the Romano-British or whether whole communities moved in. Ancient DNA has tilted the answer toward migration. Gretzinger and colleagues find up to three quarters of the ancestry in eastern England came from the continental North Sea, though it varies sharply from place to place and mixes with the resident population. English begins here, in that settlement.
contested: The migration-versus-elite-takeover debate is old and still live. Recent genomes show substantial migration rather than a thin warrior elite, but heavy Romano-British continuity and later Continental gene flow mean this is admixture, not the clean replacement seen on the steppe.
displaced: Romano-British population of eastern and southern Britain
settlers: Angles, Saxons, Jutes and Frisians from the North Sea coast
note: A proto-historic case, the same migration-or-elite-transfer question the atlas raises for the Athabaskan case. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Numic spread across the Great Basin
story: From a small homeland near the California-Nevada line, Numic-speaking people fanned out across the Great Basin over the last thousand years, the ancestors of the Shoshone, Paiute and Ute. As they spread they replaced the Fremont farmers and the other earlier peoples of the desert. It is the closest North American parallel to the Athabaskan migration, a documented ethnolinguistic turnover across a vast dry interior, ending only as horses and then settlers arrived from the east.
contested: The late Numic spread is well established from language. The mechanism is argued, competitive displacement of the Fremont in the Bettinger and Baumhoff model, versus Fremont collapse under drought followed by Numic in-filling of emptied land.
displaced: Fremont farmer-foragers and other pre-Numic Great Basin peoples
settlers: Numic (Uto-Aztecan) speakers, ancestral Shoshone, Paiute, Ute and Kawaiisu
note: An expansion case read from linguistics and archaeology, one Indigenous people spreading over another. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Kayenta migration into the southern deserts
story: When the northern Southwest emptied in the late 1200s, Kayenta people from north-eastern Arizona moved south and planted immigrant enclaves among the Hohokam and the peoples of the San Pedro and Tonto basins. At sites like Reeve Ruin and Davis Ranch they kept a distinct identity, their own perforated plates, entry-box kivas and technology, the cleanest archaeological signature of settlers who move in and hold themselves apart. The blended Salado world that followed grew out of that meeting.
contested: The migrant enclaves are widely accepted. What is debated is whether the newcomers displaced the locals or fused with them, with many reading Salado as coalescence, migrants and hosts making a new shared identity.
displaced: Local Hohokam and San Pedro / Tonto Basin populations
settlers: Kayenta migrants from the northern Southwest (ancestral Puebloan)
note: An expansion case, a rare instance where intrusive settlers left a clear material fingerprint among a host population. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Nahua (Pipil and Nicarao) migration into Central America
story: Long before the Spanish, Nahua-speaking people from central Mexico moved more than a thousand kilometres south into Central America. The Pipil settled western El Salvador and Guatemala, the Nicarao the Pacific shore of Nicaragua, founding lasting Nahua-speaking towns like Cuzcatlan among the resident Maya, Lenca and Chorotega. It was a folk migration that put down roots, not just a conquering dynasty.
contested: The migration is well attested by language and by native histories, but its timing, the number of waves, and whether the newcomers displaced or layered over the Chorotega and Maya are debated, and much of the record was written down only after the conquest.
displaced: Maya, Lenca and Oto-Manguean (Chorotega) populations of Central America
settlers: Nahua-speaking migrants (Pipil and Nicarao) from central Mexico
note: An expansion case, one of the most overlooked long-distance migrations in the Americas. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Wari and Tiwanaku colonies in Moquegua
story: In the Moquegua valley of southern Peru, two Andean states planted colonies side by side. Tiwanaku, from the shores of Lake Titicaca, sent farmers six hundred kilometres downslope to build homeland temples and cemeteries at Omo and Chen Chen. Wari, from Ayacucho, seized the Cerro Baul mesa above them and cut a canal to green the desert, a rival enclave in sight of the first. Goldstein calls the Tiwanaku settlements a true diaspora, colonists who moved and stayed for centuries, not a garrison.
contested: That both are intrusive planned colonies is not in doubt, confirmed by homeland-style building, burials and skull-shaping. What is argued is how the two states related, wary coexistence or hostility, above one shared valley.
displaced: Resident Huaracane population of the middle Moquegua valley
settlers: Tiwanaku colonists from the Titicaca basin
Wari colonists from Ayacucho
note: An expansion case, and the rare instance of two colonial powers settling one valley at once. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Saladoid settlement of the Caribbean
story: The Caribbean was colonized long before Columbus. From around 800 BCE, ceramic-making, cassava-farming people known as the Saladoid, Arawak speakers from the lower Orinoco, canoed up the island chain from Trinidad to Puerto Rico and Hispaniola. Ancient DNA now shows they did not blend with the archipelago's earlier foragers so much as replace them. Fernandes and colleagues find over ninety-eight percent of the ceramic-age ancestry was newcomer, with the older Archaic population surviving mainly in western Cuba.
contested: The near-total genetic turnover is a recent and well-supported finding, and it supersedes older models of gradual acculturation between foragers and farmers.
displaced: Archaic-age foragers of the Antilles (Ortoiroid and Casimiroid)
settlers: Saladoid (Arawak-speaking) farmers from the lower Orinoco
note: An expansion case read from ancient DNA. It reframes the Caribbean's colonization as something that began millennia before 1492. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

story: For a century the state has moved poor farmers from crowded Java, Madura and Bali to Indonesia's outer islands and settled them on land that was already someone's. It began as Dutch kolonisatie in 1905 and became a vast program under Suharto, relocating millions onto forest and customary land in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi. In Lampung the transmigrants became the majority. Dayak and other Indigenous peoples were pushed aside, and the resentment erupted in the Sampit killings of 2001.
contested: The state frames Transmigration as development and poverty relief. Critics call it internal colonization, and the recurrent violence between settlers and Indigenous peoples is widely tied to the land it took. Worldwide audit correction: Dutch-era colonisatie, New Order mass transmigration, province-specific settlement frontiers, and later decentralized or spontaneous migration have different coercive and demographic effects.
displaced: Dayak peoples of Kalimantan
Indigenous peoples of Sulawesi and Sumatra
settlers: State-sponsored Javanese, Madurese, Balinese and Sundanese settlers
note: The clearest modern non-European settler program, run by an Asian state rather than an overseas empire. West Papua is treated as its own case. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; high confidence.

name: Han colonization of the Yunnan frontier

periods.label: Linked internal sequence
periods.note: One playback stop; dated internal sequence: 1382–1644: Ming military colonization; 1644–1850: Qing migration, mining, and frontier administration.

internalSequence.label: Ming military colonization

internalSequence.note: Qing migration, mining, and frontier administration. The audit separates this phase from the other institutions and populations previously hidden inside the broad case.

story: Yunnan became part of China by settlement as much as by conquest. After the Ming took the south-west in 1382 they planted military-agricultural colonies, soldiers brought with their families, and civilian Han migrants followed for four centuries. The Tai, Yi, Bai and Hani were pushed into the uplands or absorbed as the basins around Kunming and Dali turned Han-majority. In the far south, among the Tai of Sipsong Panna, settlement stayed thin.
contested: The demographic shift is not much disputed. What scholars weigh is how much was deliberate state colonization versus commercial and refugee drift onto the frontier. Worldwide audit correction: Ming military colonies, Qing frontier administration and migration, mining booms, and suppression of local polities form multiple settlement waves over nearly five centuries.
displaced: Tai (Dai), Yi, Bai and Hani peoples of the south-west
settlers: Han military colonists and civilian migrants
note: A frontier settler process distinct from the atlas's Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang cases, and thinner in the Tai-majority far south. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

name: Tai-Ahom settlement of Assam
story: In 1228 a Tai prince named Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills from the upper Burma borderlands into the Brahmaputra valley with a few thousand followers, and the order they built lasted six hundred years. The Ahom cleared wet-rice land, bound the local Bodo-Kachari, Chutiya and Moran into a corvee-settlement system, and slowly made Assam their own even as they themselves took on Hindu ways. A small warrior-migrant elite that reshaped a valley.
contested: The history is solid. What is politically charged today is Tai-Ahom identity itself, revived and contested in modern Assam, which Yasmin Saikia traces.
displaced: Bodo-Kachari, Chutiya, Moran and Borahi peoples of the Brahmaputra valley
settlers: Tai (Ahom) migrants from the upper Burma-Yunnan borderlands
note: An eastern-India frontier case, a thin settler elite that endured and then assimilated. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.

name: Burman settlement of the Irrawaddy

periods.label: Linked internal sequence

story: The Burmans entered the Irrawaddy from the northern hills in the ninth century and made its dry heartland their own. As they built Bagan and its thousands of temples, the old Pyu city-states faded and their people were absorbed, and the Mon of the south were subordinated. The valley that had been Pyu and Mon became Burman, the demographic core of Myanmar to this day.
contested: The Pyu absorption is real, but the once-standard story of a great Mon kingdom at Thaton conquered by Bagan is challenged by Michael Aung-Thwin as a later legend. It is included partly for that dispute. Worldwide audit correction: The case infers a long demographic settlement from language, archaeology, and state formation; it does not establish one bounded displacement event or clearly identify affected predecessor communities.
displaced: Pyu city-states and Mon of the lower Irrawaddy
settlers: Burman (Bamar) migrants from the northern uplands
note: An expansion case whose founding narrative is itself contested scholarship. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

story: Japan took the southern half of Sakhalin from Russia in 1905 and made Karafuto a settler prefecture. Migrants poured in for the coal, timber and fisheries, and by the mid-1930s the population passed 300,000, overwhelmingly Japanese settlers, against roughly 2,000 Ainu, Uilta and Nivkh. Tessa Morris-Suzuki describes it as an overwhelmingly settler colony. The 1945 Soviet conquest ended it, and almost all the settlers were repatriated, the mirror image of the colony's rise.
contested: Scholarship treats Karafuto as a clear settler colony. The status of Korean labour migrants, many of them coerced, is separate from that of the Japanese settlers. Worldwide audit correction: Japanese settler colonization, Indigenous Ainu/Nivkh/Uilta dispossession, coerced Korean labor, and the 1945 Soviet takeover and population removals are distinct histories.
note: Korean labourers, many brought under coercion, are counted apart from the settler population. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; high confidence.
displaced: Ainu
Uilta (Orok)
Nivkh (Gilyak)
settlers: Japanese home-island settlers
state-assisted migrants for coal, timber and fisheries

name: Maasai expansion across the Rift Valley
story: The Maasai, Plains Nilotic pastoralists, spread south out of the Lake Turkana region across the Rift Valley from around the seventeenth century, taking the best grazing as they went. They moved into the stone-walled cattle country of the earlier Sirikwa, absorbed or drove off Southern Cushitic herders and Okiek hunter-gatherers, and in the nineteenth-century Iloikop wars the Maasai proper defeated and scattered rival Maa sections like the Kwavi and Laikipiak. Around 1850 they held a corridor from central Kenya to northern Tanzania, until the 1880s and 1890s brought rinderpest, smallpox and drought, the Mutai, and broke them.
contested: Maa-speaker expansion is well attested, but the Maasai were never one people, and much of the fighting was Maa section against Maa section. Earlier peoples were as often absorbed as replaced. It belongs here as pastoralist expansion, not a state project.
note: An expansion case of the pastoralist age. The Nandi push into the Uasin Gishu is its tail end, and the British later took the same highlands as the Kenya Highlands. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.
displaced: Sirikwa and earlier highland peoples
Southern Cushitic pastoralists
Okiek (Dorobo) hunter-gatherers
Kwavi, Laikipiak and other defeated Maa sections
settlers: Maasai (Plains Nilotic pastoralists)

name: Nandi expansion into the Uasin Gishu
story: In the middle of the nineteenth century the Nandi, a Kalenjin people of the western highlands, took the Uasin Gishu plateau from the Uasin Gishu Maasai, one of the Maasai sections. That section had already been broken in the Maasai civil wars, and the survivors were finished by the rinderpest, smallpox and drought of the 1890s. The Nandi moved into the wreckage as much as they conquered it, and held the plateau until the British seized it for white settlers around 1906.
contested: Whether the Nandi displaced the Maasai or filled land the Maasai wars and the 1890s disasters had already emptied is debated, the same question the Numic spread raises. Some accounts read parts of the plateau as earlier Nandi land retaken.
note: The tail end of the Rift Valley pastoralist wars, on highlands the British soon took as the Kenya Highlands. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.
displaced: Uasin Gishu Maasai (a defeated Maa section)
settlers: Nandi (Kalenjin, Southern Nilotic)

story: Fleeing Shaka's Zulu, Mzilikazi led his Ndebele across the Limpopo, and by 1840 had built a kingdom on the high country of what is now south-western Zimbabwe. The Ndebele settled Matabeleland, raided the Shona chiefdoms for cattle and captives, and ruled the plateau until a British column broke the kingdom in 1893 and took the land for the settlers of Rhodesia.
contested: The extent of Ndebele domination over the Shona, raiding against tribute against outright conquest, is debated, and colonial writers exaggerated it to justify their own conquest. Worldwide audit correction: The label reduces a sequence involving the Rozvi state, Kalanga communities, multiple Ndebele migrations, tribute relations, raids, and later colonial ethnic categories to a single Ndebele-versus-Shona event.
note: A pre-colonial conquest the British settlement of Rhodesia then layered over. See the Southern Rhodesia case. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

story: From about 1522 the Oromo, Cushitic pastoralists organized by the gada age-grade system, pushed north and west out of the southern lowlands into the heart of Ethiopia. Over two centuries they took much of the central highlands, settling on land emptied by the recent wars between the Christian kingdom and the sultanate of Adal, and displacing or absorbing Sidama, Damot and frontier Amhara. The sixteenth-century monk Bahrey wrote the first account of them, from the Christian side.
contested: Whether to call this migration, expansion or invasion is politically charged in Ethiopia today. Much of the land had just been emptied by the Adal wars, so the Oromo often moved into a vacuum, and assimilation ran both ways. Worldwide audit correction: Two centuries of movement, alliance, adoption, conquest, assimilation, and state formation across a vast region cannot support a single displacement arrow or a single agent–victim story.
note: An expansion case that reshaped the Ethiopian highlands before any European involvement. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.
displaced: Sidama and Damot peoples
frontier Amhara and Christian-kingdom populations

settlers: Oromo (Cushitic pastoralists of the gada system)

story: The Luo, River-Lake Nilotes, moved south out of the southern Sudan over several centuries and settled the eastern shore of Lake Victoria in what is now western Kenya. As they took the lakeshore and its fishing and grazing, they pushed the Bantu Gusii up into the highlands, absorbed other neighbours, and made Nyanza a Luo country.
contested: The Luo advance was slow and piecemeal, clan by clan, and it mixed conquest with intermarriage and absorption. It belongs here as a long Nilotic expansion, not a single campaign. Worldwide audit correction: The umbrella joins several migrations and settlements over centuries; language spread, intermarriage, political incorporation, and displacement differed across Acholi, Alur, Luo, and neighboring histories.
note: An expansion case, alongside the Maasai and Nandi movements. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.
displaced: Gusii and other Bantu of the lake basin, pushed to the highlands
earlier Kalenjin-related peoples
settlers: Luo (River-Lake Nilotes)

name: Oorlam expansion into central Namibia
story: Armed with guns, horses and ox-wagons from the Cape frontier, Afrikaans-speaking Oorlam commandos crossed the Orange River into central Namibia from the 1810s. Under Jonker Afrikaner they made Windhoek their base, subdued the Nama chiefdoms and fought the Herero for the central grazing lands through mid-century, running a raiding and cattle economy until German colonization overtook it after 1884.
contested: The Oorlam were themselves a Cape-frontier people of mixed Khoe and settler descent, so this sits between an African expansion and an outrider of Cape colonial society.
note: A pre-colonial expansion German South West Africa then displaced. See the Namibia case. Worldwide audit: retained as an exact event unit; medium confidence.
displaced: Nama (Khoekhoe) chiefdoms
Herero (Ovaherero) of the central highland
settlers: Oorlam (Orlam) commandos from the Cape frontier

name: The Fulani jihad and the Sokoto Caliphate
story: In 1804 the Fulani scholar Usman dan Fodio launched a jihad against the Hausa kings, and within a decade his followers had overthrown the Hausa city-states and built the Sokoto Caliphate, the largest state in nineteenth-century Africa. Fulani emirs took the thrones, Fulani pastoralists pressed onto Hausa and Middle Belt land, and the caliphate raided the non-Muslim south for captives until the British conquered it in 1903.
contested: The Hausa majority remained under new Fulani-led regimes. The case combines elite conquest, slave-raiding frontiers, tribute, and uneven pastoral settlement pressure rather than a uniform population replacement.
note: Included as an elite-conquest case, a deliberate contrast to the replacement expansions. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.
displaced: Hausa ruling classes of Kano, Katsina, Gobir and the other states
non-Muslim Middle Belt peoples raided for captives
settlers: Fulani emirs, scholars and pastoralist settlers

story: Around 1050 the Fatimid rulers of Egypt loosed the Bedouin tribes of the Banu Hilal and Banu Sulaym westward into Ifriqiya as a punishment on a rebellious vassal. Tens of thousands of Arab nomads poured across North Africa over the following century, wrecking the Zirid towns, turning farmland to pasture, and spreading Arabic and Bedouin ways among the Amazigh. Ibn Khaldun, four centuries later, likened them to a swarm of locusts.
contested: Ibn Khaldun's catastrophe story is now heavily qualified. Historians see the Arabization of the Maghreb as a slower cultural process, so this is a diffuse migration and language shift, one of the loosest fits in the atlas. Worldwide audit correction: Migration is historically consequential, but sweeping claims that it simply displaced or replaced Amazigh populations require regional qualification and should distinguish language shift, pastoral conflict, and state policy.
note: An expansion case of nomadic migration and cultural turnover rather than organized settlement. Worldwide audit: corrected and retained as a bounded process; medium confidence.

name: Settlement and demographic expansion of Bantu-speaking farmers through the western and central African rainforest
mechanism: demographic expansion
story: Farming populations moved gradually through and around the rainforest, mixed with some existing forager populations, and became demographically dominant in many regions. The process was neither one migration nor uniform replacement.
contested: Evidence limits and dispute: Genetic and archaeological chronologies remain uneven, and modern language identity cannot be projected unchanged into the deep past.

name: Settlement of the Great Lakes region by Bantu-speaking farmers and ironworkers
mechanism: demographic expansion
story: Bantu-speaking farming and ironworking communities established durable settlements around the Great Lakes. Their interaction with Kansyore and other fisher-foragers, Batwa-related forest communities, and pastoralists included exchange and admixture as well as absorption, displacement, and marginalization.
contested: Evidence limits and dispute: Urewe and Kansyore are archaeological traditions rather than ethnic names, and modern population identities cannot be projected unchanged into the deep past.

name: Settlement and demographic expansion of Bantu-speaking farmers through eastern Africa
mechanism: demographic expansion
story: Bantu-speaking farmers established settlements through the Kenya–Tanzania interior and along the eastern African coast over many centuries. They encountered a mosaic of Kansyore and other foragers and Pastoral Neolithic herders; the resulting histories included coexistence and admixture as well as absorption, displacement, and confinement to less productive land.

periods.label: Linked internal sequence

internalSequence.label: Haabets Koloni and the Bergen company
internalSequence.note: Egede's expedition established Haabets Koloni at Kangeq under crown authorization and Bergen merchant organization. This began the sustained mission-and-trade project among nearby Kalaallit communities.

internalSequence.label: Crown support, mission growth, and Jacob Severin's monopoly
internalSequence.note: The Crown and successive licensed operators sustained the small colonial network. European personnel remained a thin posted stratum; Greenlandic production remained essential to the trade. A 1733 smallpox outbreak caused severe local mortality, but no compatible population denominator survives for event-wide scoring.

internalSequence.label: Expanded monopoly network before the 1782 Instrux
internalSequence.note: Successive monopoly institutions extended the colony-town and trade-station network. The 1782 Instrux introduced a more formalized and separationist administrative regime.

story: Beginning in 1721, Danish-Norwegian crown-backed missionaries and successive monopoly companies established a network of small colonial towns and mission-and-trade stations in West Greenland. These externally governed nodes exercised institutional control over land and organized trade and mission activity around nearby Kalaallit communities. European personnel remained few and were largely posted for fixed terms, while Greenlandic producers sustained the colonial trade. This was colonial incorporation, not mass European settler replacement.
contested: Evidence limits and dispute: The evidence does not establish coast-wide occupation, Indigenous tenure extinguishment, mass removal, or Indigenous cession. Danish-Norwegian elites justified the project partly through an asserted continuity with medieval Norwegian rule; that was a colonial rationale, not evidence of unbroken Scandinavian occupation or Kalaallit consent. A 1733 smallpox outbreak followed the return of a Greenlander from Denmark and caused severe local mortality around Godthåb, but the available account supplies no denominator for the affected network. The 1925 Ittoqqortoormiit movement, 1953–55 Inughuit removal, post-1782 separation and assimilation regimes, East Greenland's later incorporation, and later constitutional transitions occurred under later regimes and are not part of this 1721–1782 chronology.
displaced: Kalaallit and other Inuit communities living near the West Greenland colony-town, mission, and trade network
settlers: The Danish-Norwegian Crown
Hans Egede and crown-backed mission institutions
Successive monopoly companies, merchants, and posted colonial personnel

story: Crop failure and food shortage struck Las Humanas from 1667. A contemporary Franciscan report attributed more than 450 deaths there to starvation in 1668, while the later NPS history describes the total more cautiously as perhaps 450. An Apache attack seriously damaged the mission in September 1670. The Franciscans probably closed it in 1671, and surviving residents moved through Abó toward Piro-speaking Rio Grande missions, probably Isleta, by 1672. Las Humanas was not durably replaced by an incoming community and remained abandoned until reoccupation of the area after 1800.
contested: Evidence limits and dispute: The death report, later population statements, and raid losses do not supply compatible denominators and cannot yield a mortality share or displacement total. Drought, famine, disease, Spanish extraction and consolidation, and Apache attack interacted. The evidence does not show a single-cause Apache conquest or replacement settlement.

story: In early December 1761 Spanish officials decided to move Sobaipuri-O'odham residents from San Pedro communities to reinforce Soamca, Guevavi, and Bac, consolidate frontier defense, and bring more people under mission control. Captain Francisco Elías executed the order by March 1762 amid sustained Apache pressure. His report counted 250 people settled or enumerated at Tucson and said missionary and Indigenous officials had reported about 400; people not enumerated were described as moving among nearby towns. Thirty families are separately documented at Soamca, and activity is documented at Sonoita. These figures and places do not form one complete partition and are not combined. The order and substantial partial relocation are established; complete valley abandonment is not.
contested: Evidence limits and dispute: Sayre and Spicer describe an emptied lower San Pedro, while Seymour's archaeological interpretation reports O'odham occupations after 1762. The evidence supports substantial outward movement but leaves complete abandonment, durable exclusion, and Apache replacement unresolved. Soamca, Guevavi, and Bac were intended destinations; Tucson and Soamca are directly documented execution outcomes, while Sonoita and surrounding towns appear in the wider movement record. Spanish compulsion is the proximate mechanism; Apache pressure is an interacting condition.
displaced: The documented subset of Sobaipuri-O'odham residents ordered from San Pedro Valley communities
settlers: Governor José Tienda de Cuervo and Spanish frontier officers
