Jews were also affected by expulsions of British and French nationals; about 500 Jews of other nationalities were expelled; roughly 460 Jewish-owned businesses were sequestered; and many people lost jobs or faced citizenship pressure. The World Jewish Congress recorded 14,102 Jewish departures between 22 November 1956 and 15 March 1957, most of them to Israel according to Joel Beinin.
contested: The detainee, nationality, expulsion, business, job-loss, and departure counts overlap and must not be added. The military property-seizure proclamation was rescinded on 27 April 1957 for Jews who were not British or French citizens, and some property was returned. Slower migration after mid-1957 is aftermath rather than part of this bounded event.
displaced: Egyptian Jews detained, expelled, deprived of work or property, or pressured to leave during the Suez crisis
14,102 recorded Jewish departures during the peak interval; categories overlap
settlers: Egyptian detention, expulsion, nationality, employment, and sequestration authorities
British, French, and Israeli forces as the war trigger, not the administrators of Egyptian measures
placeGloss: The segmented routes show Israel as the documented majority destination in the peak 1956–1957 departure, not a complete person-by-person destination census.
evidence: published historical synthesis drawing on contemporary records, with exact peak-departure and partial-reversal dates

name: Wartime detention and release-linked Jewish departure from Egypt
mechanism: wartime arrest, harsh detention, citizenship-tiered release, and release-linked exit
affectedLabel: Detained / departing
actorLabel: Authorities / intermediaries

internalSequence.label: Wartime arrests and departure of foreign citizens
Resumed small-group release of stateless detainees
Final citizen detainees and families leave under no-return conditions

story: In the first hours of the June 1967 war, President Gamal Abdel Nasser ordered arrests that imprisoned about 500 Egyptian Jewish men. Foreign citizens were released and left during 1967–1968; releases of stateless and Egyptian citizens resumed in April 1969. The final group—about 80 Egyptian-citizen men—and their families were permitted to leave only after the prisoners promised to renounce Egyptian citizenship and not return. All prisoners had been freed by March 1971.
contested: The evidence does not provide a complete detainee or family roster, prison assignments, individual departure dates, or final destinations. Published estimates of the Jewish population remaining in Egypt before the arrests differ, so the proportion arrested is unresolved. France was a documented receiving and negotiating channel—102 Jews had reached Paris by 2 May 1969—but the mapped route does not claim that Paris was everyone’s final home. The explicit citizenship-renunciation and no-return condition is documented for the final group of about 80 Egyptian-citizen men and their families, not automatically for every detainee.
displaced: About 500 Egyptian Jewish men arrested during and after the June 1967 war
Family members whose departure accompanied the staged releases
settlers: President Nasser and Egyptian military, security, foreign-ministry, and interior-ministry authorities
French, Spanish, Italian, Greek, ICRC, UNHCR, and Israeli intermediaries in the release negotiations
placeGloss: The route to Paris represents a documented receiving channel and the 102 arrivals reported by 2 May 1969; ultimate destinations were broader and incompletely resolved.
evidence: archival historical study with staged-release dates, citizenship categories, and a documented Paris arrival count

name: British deportation from Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
mechanism: British seizure, resident deportation, and settlement destruction
affectedLabel: Residents / refugees
actorLabel: Forces / authorities

internalSequence.label: British seizure, deportation to France, and destruction of homes
French restoration and permitted resident return

story: In September 1778, a British expedition under Newfoundland governor John Montagu seized Saint-Pierre and Miquelon. The inhabitants were sent to France and their homes destroyed. Personal refugee files document property losses and families living in French ports. The islands were restored to France in 1783 and residents were allowed to return, closing this removal interval before the separate 1793 seizure.
contested: The opened evidence does not provide a complete deportee count, household roster, vessel-by-vessel route, inventory of losses, or return rate. The route therefore ends at a broad French Channel receiving region rather than claiming one destination for every person. The 1783 restoration and permission to return are the event boundary, not proof that every displaced resident returned.
displaced: French and Acadian-background residents of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon sent to France after the 1778 seizure
Households whose homes, fishing establishments, and possessions were destroyed or abandoned
settlers: Newfoundland governor John Montagu and the British expedition
British imperial authorities administering the wartime seizure and removal

targets.name: French Channel ports — broad receiving region

placeGloss: The transatlantic routes show France as the documented deportation destination. Their endpoint represents the French Channel ports named across the refugee files, not a complete destination census.
evidence: historical synthesis and archival refugee-file study with direct evidence of removal to France, losses, and intended 1783 re-establishment

name: Second British deportation of Saint-Pierre and Miquelon
mechanism: British seizure, phased deportation, fisheries occupation, and wartime depopulation
affectedLabel: Prisoners / deportees
actorLabel: Forces / authorities

internalSequence.label: British seizure and removal of officials, troops, and seasonal fishermen
Evacuation of the 950 resident inhabitants
Town destruction and deserted interval before the 1816 return

story: A British expedition from Halifax seized Saint-Pierre and Miquelon in May 1793. James Ogilvie returned to Halifax with 570 officials, troops, and fishermen as prisoners. The 950 resident inhabitants remained until orders removed them in 1794 to Nova Scotia and the Channel Islands. English fishermen then used the islands’ facilities; when a French squadron appeared in 1796, the English withdrew and the French destroyed the town. The islands remained deserted until French possession and resident settlement were re-established in 1816.
contested: The 570 prisoners removed in 1793 and the 950 resident inhabitants removed in 1794 are different measured groups and are not added into a single population estimate. The sources do not provide a complete household roster, destination allocation, property-loss inventory, or return rate. Landry’s introduction prints 1791 for the second conquest; the event uses 1793 because Janzen, the Dictionary of Canadian Biography, and the French overseas archives independently support that date. The end year 1815 is the last full deserted year before repopulation in 1816.
displaced: 570 officials, troops, and seasonal fishermen taken to Halifax in 1793
950 resident inhabitants ordered removed in 1794 to Nova Scotia and the Channel Islands
settlers: James Ogilvie, Captain William Affleck, and the British expedition and authorities
English fishermen using island facilities after the removals
Rear-Admiral de Richery and the French squadron responsible for the 1796 destruction
placeGloss: Halifax is the documented 1793 prisoner destination. The second endpoint represents the Channel Islands as a documented 1794 destination region; the sources do not allocate every resident between Nova Scotia and the islands.
evidence: independent historical syntheses, an official archival chronology, and biographical research identifying the phased removals, receiving regions, and deserted interval

name: Ottoman Circassian settlement on the Vidin–Niš–Sofia frontier
mechanism: state-directed refugee placement and strategic frontier settlement
affectedLabel: Refugees / affected communities
actorLabel: Authorities / settlers

internalSequence.label: Refugee arrivals and frontier allocation, peaking in 1864
Village establishment and initial resource allocation

story: Between 1862 and 1867, the Ottoman Refugee Commission and provincial authorities placed Circassian refugee households in new villages across the Vidin, Niš, and Sofia frontier districts. Many arrived through the Black Sea ports of Varna and Constanța. The state intended the settlement belt to reinforce Ottoman authority and form a strategic barrier near Serbia. Local Christian and Muslim residents supplied transport, housing, provisions, and other resources, and some land was reassigned.
contested: The available figures describe the Danube Vilayet as a whole or give example village sizes; they do not establish a population total for this frontier tract and are not added together. Local burdens and land contention are documented, but general resident removal is not. The interval describes arrival and initial allocation, not the lifetime of the resulting villages, and post-1877 secondary migration is a separate process.
displaced: Circassian refugee households expelled from or fleeing the northwest Caucasus
Local Christian and Muslim communities supplying land, transport, housing, and provisions
settlers: Ottoman Refugee Commission and provincial, military, and local authorities
Circassian households assigned to the Vidin–Niš–Sofia frontier belt
placeGloss: The map connects the refugees’ broad northwest-Caucasus homeland to the documented frontier destination belt. Varna and Constanța were important transit ports, but the lines do not claim a household-by-household route census.
evidence: specialist historical study documenting the arrival interval, Ottoman administration, transit ports, frontier districts, strategic rationale, village placement, and local provisioning burdens

name: Ottoman Circassian agricultural settlement along the Danube and in Dobruja
mechanism: state-directed refugee placement, farmland allocation, and land surveying
affectedLabel: Refugees / affected communities
actorLabel: Authorities / settlers

internalSequence.label: Refugee arrivals and agricultural village placement
Land mapping and allocation, especially in Dobruja
End of the bounded initial-placement interval

story: From 1862 to 1867, Ottoman authorities placed Circassian refugee households in new villages and smaller groups in existing settlements along the Danube near Lom, Nikopol, and Svishtov and in Dobruja. Officials allocated farmland and undertook land mapping in 1865–1866, especially in Dobruja. Local Christian and Muslim agricultural communities supplied land, housing, provisions, and labor to the program.
contested: The source reports only vilayet-wide totals, not a population or durable village roster for this agricultural tract. The 8,000 Abkhazians reported arriving in the vilayet in 1867 cannot be assigned to these destinations. Documented land, labor, and provisioning burdens do not by themselves prove that local residents were removed. This is a geographic and land-use branch of the same wider administration, not a claim of a wholly separate bureaucracy.
displaced: Circassian refugees placed in the Danube corridor and Dobruja
Local Christian and Muslim agricultural communities whose land, housing, provisions, or labor supported the program
settlers: Ottoman Refugee Commission, Danube Vilayet authorities, and land-survey officials
Circassian refugee households assigned to agricultural settlements
placeGloss: The map shows the broad northwest-Caucasus homeland and the documented Danube and Dobruja destination tract. Black Sea transit is documented, but the lines do not assign every household to a specific port or village.
evidence: specialist historical study documenting the arrival interval, destination corridor, village forms, agricultural allocation, Dobruja land survey, and local provisioning obligations

name: Ottoman settlement of North Caucasian refugees in Uzunyayla
mechanism: collective state-directed refugee placement and land allocation
affectedLabel: Refugees / affected communities
actorLabel: Authorities / settlers

internalSequence.label: Collective placement on the Uzunyayla plateau
Initial consolidation and continuing land conflict

story: During the 1860s, Ottoman authorities collectively settled Circassian and other North Caucasian refugee cohorts on the Uzunyayla plateau using miri, vakıf, and land classified as vacant. The principal placement was reported complete in 1864. Afshar pasture was assigned to newcomers, conflict followed, and the fields and property of settled cultivators were also affected as the new villages took shape.
contested: The 1860–1870 span marks settlement formation, not uninterrupted migration for a decade. Nearly 3,000 households refers to Sivas province rather than securely to Uzunyayla; 318 households and 2,201 people describe an unsettled remainder at one checkpoint and are not added to it. The source does not provide a complete household-to-village register or prove that every named cohort remained throughout the interval.
displaced: Circassian and other North Caucasian refugee cohorts assigned to Uzunyayla
Afshar pastoralists and settled cultivators whose pasture, fields, property, water, or materials were affected
settlers: Ottoman central, Refugee Commission, Aziziye, and Kayseri authorities
North Caucasian refugee households placed in collective settlements
placeGloss: The broad route connects the refugees’ Caucasus homeland to Uzunyayla. The source does not support a more detailed intermediate itinerary or a village-by-village route map.
evidence: specialist historical study documenting collective placement, land categories, the 1864 milestone, cohort composition, and conflict over pasture, fields, and property

name: Circassian settlement at Wadi al-Sir
mechanism: refugee village foundation within Ottoman land-allotment and registration institutions
affectedLabel: Refugees / affected communities
actorLabel: Authorities / settlers

internalSequence.label: Circassian village foundation at Wadi al-Sir

story: Circassian refugees founded Wadi al-Sir in 1880 within the Ottoman system of refugee settlement, land allotment, miri registration, and agricultural development in the Balqa. The resulting village entered a regional landscape of pasture claims, cultivation, and later property exchange. The state's role operated through law, land allocation, and infrastructure rather than a documented direct removal order against a predecessor community.
contested: The ultimate northwest-Caucasus origin is documented, but the settlers’ immediate route may have passed through Anatolia or the post-1877 Balkans and is unresolved. Later records identify Bzhedugh and Abzakh quarters but do not prove that both groups jointly founded the village in 1880. No Wadi-specific predecessor community, forced removal, village population, or direct command placement is established; Transjordan-wide totals and land-price figures are not used as local population counts.
displaced: Circassian refugees establishing Wadi al-Sir
Regional Balqa land and pasture claimants affected by registration and cultivation; no named removed predecessor is documented
settlers: Ottoman refugee and Balqa land authorities
Circassian refugee households founding the village

origins.name: Northwest Caucasus — ultimate origin; immediate route unresolved

placeGloss: The long line shows only the settlers’ ultimate northwest-Caucasus origin. It does not claim a direct journey or choose between possible intermediate residence in Anatolia and the Balkans.
evidence: specialist historical study documenting the 1880 foundation, Ottoman refugee and miri-land framework, registration, cultivation, and later property evidence

name: Bikini nuclear-test displacement and return
mechanism: nuclear-test land clearance, serial compelled relocation, unsafe return, and renewed removal
affectedLabel: Removed / returning
actorLabel: Authorities / carriers

internalSequence.label: About 167 Bikini people removed to Rongerik before nuclear testing
Serial relocation through Kwajalein, Kili, and Jaluit
Federal safety assurance followed by partial return to Bikini
Renewed removal to Kili and Ejit after dangerous radioactivity was found

story: United States authorities removed about 167 Bikini people from their atoll in March 1946 so it could be used for nuclear testing. Rongerik could not support the community, and later moves carried people through Kwajalein, Kili, and Jaluit. After a 1967 federal safety assurance, some residents returned to Bikini beginning in 1971. Monitoring later found dangerous radioactivity, and the returnees were removed again in 1978 to Kili and Ejit.
contested: The figure of about 167 belongs only to the March 1946 removal. The later moves, returns, and renewed removals involve overlapping subsets whose complete rosters and totals are not available, so they are not added together. The 1967 assurance preceded a return; it does not establish that Bikini was safe. The map shows only documented movement links and does not assign an exact route to every person.
displaced: About 167 Bikini people removed in March 1946
Overlapping later groups moved among Rongerik, Kwajalein, Kili, Jaluit, Bikini, and Ejit
settlers: United States Navy, occupying administration, and Trust Territory authorities responsible for testing and removal
United States radiological and resettlement authorities responsible for safety assurances, monitoring, and renewed removal
placeGloss: The segmented lines follow documented removal links between the Bikini homeland and receiving places. They summarize the community chain rather than claim one itinerary for every person; the 1971 return is described but not given an invented point of departure.
evidence: an authoritative recent United Nations synthesis with separate paragraphs for the initial removal, serial relocations, safety assurance, partial return, and renewed removal

name: Enewetak nuclear-test displacement and return
mechanism: nuclear-test requisition, compelled removal to Ujelang, cleanup, and organized homeland return
affectedLabel: Removed / returning
actorLabel: Authorities / community

internalSequence.label: Enewetak polity removed to Ujelang for nuclear testing
Cleanup, decontamination, and resettlement preparation
Organized return to Enewetak, Medren, and Japtan

story: United States authorities requisitioned Enewetak Atoll for nuclear testing and moved the Enewetak polity to Ujelang in December 1947. The community endured prolonged exile and petitioned to return. After cleanup and decontamination from 1977 to 1980, Enewetak people returned to Enewetak, Medren, and Japtan within their southern-atoll homeland.
contested: The United Nations report gives one combined 500-person return figure for the Enewetak and Enjebi polities. It does not provide an Enewetak-only count, and no portion of the shared figure is assigned here. The record also does not give a complete household roster or island-by-island duration of return.
displaced: Members of the Enewetak polity removed to Ujelang
Enewetak people returning in 1980 to islands within their southern-atoll homeland
settlers: United States Navy and Trust Territory authorities responsible for requisition and removal
United States defense, energy, and interior agencies responsible for cleanup, radiological assessment, and resettlement
placeGloss: The outward segment shows the 1947 removal to Ujelang; the return segment ends in the Enewetak polity’s documented 1980 southern-atoll return area. Enjebi’s separate homeland and unresolved return are not folded into this map.
evidence: United Nations and United States government records distinguishing the Enewetak polity, the December 1947 move to Ujelang, the 1977–1980 cleanup, and the 1980 southern-atoll return

name: Enjebi nuclear-test displacement and blocked homeland return
mechanism: nuclear-test requisition, compelled removal to Ujelang, resettlement outside the homeland, and blocked homeland return
affectedLabel: Removed / claimants
actorLabel: Authorities / community

internalSequence.label: Enjebi polity removed to Ujelang for nuclear testing
Community vote to return to the Enjebi homeland
Resettlement only on islands within the Enewetak polity’s homeland
United Nations report records continuing displacement from Enjebi

story: United States authorities removed the distinct Enjebi polity from its northern Enewetak Atoll homeland to Ujelang in December 1947. Enjebi people voted in 1979 to return home, but the combined 1980 resettlement placed them only on decontaminated islands within the Enewetak polity’s southern homeland. Federal agencies disagreed about Enjebi’s habitability, Congress did not fund homeland resettlement, and the United Nations reported in 2025 that the Enjebi people remained displaced.
contested: No terminal year is supported. The combined 500-person 1980 return figure covers both the Enewetak and Enjebi polities and cannot be converted into an Enjebi count. The map shows resettlement outside the Enjebi homeland and leaves the attempted homeland return visibly incomplete; it does not imply that Enjebi was restored.
displaced: The Enjebi polity removed from its northern-atoll homeland to Ujelang
Enjebi people resettled only on islands in the Enewetak polity’s homeland while maintaining a homeland-return claim
settlers: United States Navy and Trust Territory authorities responsible for requisition and removal
United States defense, energy, and interior agencies and Congress as cleanup, habitability, and funding actors
placeGloss: The map shows the 1947 removal to Ujelang and the 1980 resettlement on islands within the Enewetak polity’s homeland. There is deliberately no completed line back to Enjebi: the homeland-return claim remained unresolved.
evidence: United Nations and United States government records distinguishing the Enjebi polity and homeland, the 1947 move, the 1979 vote, the constrained 1980 resettlement, and continuing displacement

name: Castle Bravo displacement of the Rongelapese
mechanism: fallout exposure, delayed evacuation, unsafe return authorization, and community-requested re-evacuation
affectedLabel: Exposed / displaced
actorLabel: Authorities / carriers

internalSequence.label: Castle Bravo exposure and delayed United States evacuation
Displacement through Kwajalein and Ejit
United States-authorized return to Rongelap
Community-requested evacuation to Mejatto carried by Greenpeace

story: Castle Bravo fallout exposed 82 Rongelapese on Rongelap and Ailinginae in March 1954. United States authorities evacuated them only after a delay, first to Kwajalein and then to Ejit. A government-authorized return to Rongelap followed in 1957, joined by about 200 Rongelapese who had been absent during the test. After later health concerns and unsuccessful relocation requests, the community sought evacuation; Greenpeace carried the 300 remaining residents from Rongelap to Mejatto in 1985.
contested: The 82 exposed residents, about 200 additional 1957 returnees, and 300 people moved in 1985 are phase-specific, overlapping figures and must never be summed. The sources do not provide a complete person-level roster or identify where each absent 1957 returnee came from. The United States made the testing, delayed-evacuation, and return-safety decisions; the Rongelapese community requested the 1985 movement and Greenpeace carried it.
displaced: 82 Rongelapese exposed on Rongelap and Ailinginae in 1954
About 200 additional Rongelapese joining the 1957 return
300 remaining residents evacuated from Rongelap to Mejatto in 1985; the phase figures overlap
settlers: United States nuclear-testing, Trust Territory, medical, and radiological authorities
The Rongelapese community as evacuation petitioners and Greenpeace as the 1985 carrier
placeGloss: The ordered segments show the documented community chain. Ailinginae is marked at atoll scale because the report does not identify the occupied islet. No route is invented for the approximately 200 people who were absent during Castle Bravo and joined the 1957 return.
evidence: an authoritative recent United Nations synthesis distinguishing the 1954 exposure and evacuation, the Kwajalein and Ejit displacement, the 1957 return, and the community-requested 1985 evacuation

name: Mbelwa Ngoni conquest and settlement in northern Malawi
mechanism: armed movement, conquest, captive incorporation, and durable settlement
affectedLabel: Subjected / incorporated
actorLabel: Movers / rulers

internalSequence.label: Mbelwa installed at Ng’onga in the Henga Valley; the group moves south
Tumbuka subjection, destruction of the remaining Chikulamayembe state, and settlement near the Rukuru–Kasitu–Ruzi confluence before Choma
Mpherembe’s faction joins Mbelwa after its separate northeastern-Zambia sequence

story: Around 1855, after Mbelwa’s installation at Ng’onga in the Henga Valley, his Ngoni followers moved south into the northern Malawi highlands. They reduced most Tumbuka communities to subjection, destroyed the remaining Chikulamayembe state, and settled for several years near the confluence of the Rukuru, Kasitu, and Ruzi rivers before moving to Choma. The polity incorporated captives and was later joined by Mpherembe’s distinct, semi-independent faction in the early 1870s.
contested: No source fixes an exact day or year for the whole sequence. The playback coordinate is therefore an explicitly approximate c. 1855, not the model’s 1858 proxy. The evidence does not provide a population count, a complete captive roster, a uniform land-transfer mechanism, or proof that all Tumbuka residents were removed. Subjection and incorporation were central outcomes; this is not presented as total demographic replacement.
displaced: Tumbuka communities subjected during the southward movement
The remaining Chikulamayembe political order
Male and female captives incorporated from encountered and neighboring communities
settlers: Mbelwa and his Ngoni followers
Mtwalo and Mabilabo’s associated segments
Mpherembe’s later-joining faction and Ngoni age regiments
placeGloss: The short route follows the source-described southward sequence from Ng’onga in the Henga Valley to the temporary confluence settlement and then Choma. The Mpherembe branch is retained in the dated narrative but receives no invented line from a generalized northeastern-Zambia origin.
evidence: McCracken’s synthesis, Thompson’s specialist study, and Nyirenda’s University of Malawi research supporting the approximate chronology, southward sequence, Tumbuka subjection, Chikulamayembe destruction, settlement locations, captive incorporation, and later Mpherembe junction; McCracken cites Thompson for this history and the two are not counted as independent attestations

name: Dutch Cape expansion and Khoikhoi land-and-labor dispossession
mechanism: colonial land grants, pastoral dispossession, conquest, and labor incorporation
affectedLabel: Dispossessed / incorporated
actorLabel: Colonial agents / settlers

internalSequence.label: The VOC establishes the Table Bay provisioning station
Free-burgher grants occupy choice Khoikhoi pasturage along the Liesbeek
The first Khoikhoi–Dutch war ends with a VOC claim to land by conquest
Agrarian and loan-farm expansion extends into Stellenbosch, Paarl, and Swartland
Second British occupation ends the bounded Dutch institutional phase

story: The VOC station founded at Table Bay in 1652 became an agrarian and pastoral colony. Grants beginning in 1657 occupied watered Khoikhoi pasturage; war, conquest claims, expanding farms, and loss of herds and independent subsistence progressively dispossessed communities around the southwestern Cape. Survivors followed different paths, including resistance and migration, while many became clients or low-status laborers on settler farms.
contested: The sources establish the territorial and labor relationship but do not provide a parcel-by-parcel land history, annual population estimates, or a complete record of individual labor status. The 1806 endpoint is a change of colonial regime, not an end to dispossession. Imported African and Asian slave labor was historically important at the Cape but is outside this Khoikhoi-bounded event, so it is not counted in this case’s imported-labor measure.
displaced: Khoikhoi pastoral communities around Table Bay and the expanding southwestern Cape frontier
People who lost grazing land, water access, herds, and independent means of subsistence
Survivors incorporated as settler clients and low-status farm laborers
settlers: Dutch East India Company officials and garrison personnel
Free burghers, agricultural settlers, and later pastoral loan-farm holders
placeGloss: The long segment identifies the VOC colonial founding stream. The shorter Cape segments show the source-described progression from Table Bay grants into the southwestern agrarian and pastoral frontier; they do not claim a single annual march or uniform removal route.
evidence: Guelke and Shell’s land-and-water analysis, Adhikari’s frontier chronology, and the frozen South African History Online source row support the institutional sequence, alienation of Khoikhoi pasturage, and incorporation of survivors while leaving local counts and parcel histories unresolved

name: Cape San clearance under trekboer and commando expansion
mechanism: pastoral invasion, game depletion, water and foraging disruption, commando killing, displacement, and captive seizure
affectedLabel: Cleared / displaced / captured
actorLabel: Settlers / commandos

internalSequence.label: Pastoral frontier reaches San country beyond the cultivable southwestern Cape
An officially sanctioned all-burgher commando operates
Compulsory commando duty formalizes frontier mobilization
Sustained open war combines killing, captive taking, and land seizure
Second British occupation marks the atlas cutoff; violence and dispossession continued

story: From about 1700, trekboer pastoral expansion carried the Cape frontier into San hunting country. Settlers depleted game, disrupted water, grazing, and foraging resources, and organized official and unofficial commandos. By the later eighteenth century recurrent raids killed San people, drove survivors toward more arid country, and seized women and children as forced farm labor while settlers occupied the cleared frontier.
contested: Colonial records do not supply a complete victim or captive census, and their shifting use of San, Khoikhoi, and Khoisan labels can blur identities at the frontier. The evidence documents both official and unofficial commandos but does not make every raid centrally ordered. The c. 1700 onset is approximate, and 1806 is a colonial-regime cutoff rather than the end of violence or land loss.
displaced: San communities across the expanding Cape pastoral frontier
People killed or driven from hunting grounds after game depletion and disruption of water and foraging resources
Women and children seized in commando raids for local farm labor
settlers: Trekboer pastoral settlers occupying water and grazing land
Official and unofficial burgher commandos
VOC authorities that supplied, sanctioned, or tolerated the commando system
placeGloss: The route depicts the broad eastward and northeastward expansion of an already established Cape pastoral frontier. It is not a transoceanic migration line and does not assign every commando to the same path or year.
evidence: Adhikari’s book and article provide the frontier and commando chronology, relationship among land seizure, lethal violence, and captive taking, and the limits of colonial identity labels; the frozen South African History Online source row corroborates the pre-1806 San-specific mechanism

name: Han conquest and soldier-farmer colonization of the Hexi Corridor
mechanism: military conquest, commanderies, defenses, and soldier-farmer colonies
affectedLabel: Conquered / locally affected
actorLabel: Han state / colonists

internalSequence.label: Han armies conquer the Hexi Corridor; Wuwei and Jiuquan become commandery seats
Zhangye becomes a commandery seat as the corridor system expands
Defenses and tuntian soldier-farmer colonies spread from the eastern corridor toward Dunhuang
The fall of Han marks the atlas cutoff, not an exact end for every colony

story: After Han armies conquered the Hexi Corridor in 121 BCE, the state established commandery seats, defensive works, and military-agricultural colonies along its oases. Around Wuwei, burials suggest soldiers or newly arrived soldier-farmers, some with immediate family members; elsewhere, the evidence traces military-farming colonies and control west through Zhangye and Jiuquan toward Dunhuang. Under tuntian, soldier-farmers supplied grain for government envoys traveling toward the Western Regions and defended and colonized the frontier.
contested: The sources establish conquest, state institutions, and durable colonization, but they do not provide resident-removal totals, parcel transfers, settler counts, or the fate of each Xiongnu or oasis community. The public family is therefore Conquest and incorporation, while the frozen v5 statistical row retains its earlier Settler replacement assignment until the next release. The 220 CE endpoint is a dynastic transition bound, not a simultaneous end to every installation.
displaced: Xiongnu political control conquered in the Hexi Corridor
Local corridor and oasis communities whose specific land and demographic outcomes remain unresolved
settlers: Han armies and commandery administrations
Military-farming colonists along the corridor; Wuwei-area burials include newly arrived soldier-farmers and some immediate family members
placeGloss: The first line begins at a deliberately coarse middle–Yellow River point representing the Chinese heartland, not a documented departure city for every settler. The corridor sequence shows the source-supported westward institutional and colonial geography; it is not a claim that one cohort marched through every commandery in one journey.
evidence: Clydesdale’s archaeological synthesis supports Wuwei and Jiuquan in 121 BCE, Zhangye in 111 BCE, the soldier-farmer colonies, tuntian’s defense-and-colonization role, and the 220 CE transition; Wen independently supports the 121 BCE conquest, following-decade administrative seats through Dunhuang, and defensive construction

name: Han forced migration and tuntian garrisons in the Western Regions
mechanism: imperial forced migration into self-sufficient military-agricultural outposts
affectedLabel: Compelled migrants / local peoples
actorLabel: Han state / garrisons

internalSequence.label: Emperor Wu orders thousands from the North China Plain to establish western tuntian outposts

story: In 101 BCE Emperor Wu ordered thousands of people from the North China Plain to migrate to the western fringes of the Han empire and establish large, self-sufficient tuntian outposts. These military-agricultural garrisons projected political, military, and economic power toward Central Asian kingdoms. At Shichengzi, probably ancient Shule, burials and crop remains suggest a community that probably mixed Han migrants with local agro-pastoralists.
contested: The source identifies forcible migration, a 101 BCE start, and at least 45 Han-period city sites catalogued in Xinjiang, not all identified as tuntian outposts. It does not give a program-wide endpoint, the route or household composition of every migrant cohort, or the effects on specific local peoples. Shichengzi’s reported abandonment in 75 CE is site-specific and is not used as the end of the wider program. The primary-family label records state-directed population placement; it does not imply demonstrated removal of every pre-existing oasis community.
displaced: Thousands of Han people ordered to migrate from the North China Plain
Local agro-pastoralist peoples whose interactions and territorial outcomes remain unresolved
settlers: Emperor Wu and the Han state
Military-garrison personnel and state-directed migrants at western outposts
placeGloss: Shichengzi is the securely located site example, not a stand-in for every Han-period city site catalogued in Xinjiang. The long line visualizes the documented program-level movement from the North China Plain; the source does not preserve each cohort’s exact route.
evidence: Sheng and colleagues directly support the 101 BCE imperial order, thousands of migrants from the North China Plain, large self-sufficient western tuntian garrisons, at least 45 Han-period city sites catalogued in Xinjiang, Shichengzi’s location and probable mixed population, and the unresolved character of local interaction and the wider program endpoint

name: Foundation of Sybaris and subjection of neighboring communities
mechanism: colonial foundation, agrarian expansion, and political subjection
affectedLabel: Subjected / territorially affected
actorLabel: Colonists / ruling polis
story: Sybaris was founded around 720 BCE as an Achaean and Troezenian colony near the Crati River. Strabo’s foundation account names Is of Helice and says that the city later ruled four neighboring tribes and twenty-five subject cities. The atlas treats that expansion as part of Sybaris’s territorial formation, while keeping the much later Crotonian destruction of Sybaris in 510 BCE outside this event.
contested: The sources do not date each stage of expansion, name the four neighboring tribes, map the twenty-five-city network, or separate alliance, tribute, coercion, land transfer, and resident removal for every dependency. The c. 720 BCE stop dates the foundation, not the completion of the chora or subject network, and the family does not imply that every subjected community was displaced.
displaced: Four unnamed neighboring tribes reported as coming under Sybarite rule
Communities in the reported network of twenty-five subject cities whose local outcomes remain unresolved
settlers: Achaean and Troezenian colonists
Is of Helice and the early Sybarite polis
placeGloss: The route identifies the Achaean origin named in Strabo’s foundation account. It does not reconstruct a ship track, represent every Troezenian participant, or map the later subject network whose boundaries are unresolved.
evidence: Lomas supplies the modern c. 720 BCE foundation date and Achaean/Troezenian identification; Strabo 6.1.13 supplies Is of Helice, the Achaean foundation, and the later report of four neighboring tribes and twenty-five subject cities

name: Traditional account of Ionian capture of Chonian Siris
mechanism: literary tradition of refugee migration and forceful occupation of a pre-existing city
affectedLabel: Chonian residents in the literary tradition
actorLabel: Ionian refugees in the literary tradition
dates: traditionally c. 660 BCE; archaeological chronology disputed
story: Strabo preserves a literary account in which Ionian refugees fleeing Lydian rule took the Chonian city of Siris by force and called it Polieium. Other ancient testimony identifies the Ionians as people from Colophon. Synchronizing that tradition with Gyges’ conquest of Colophon produces a conventional date around 660 BCE, but the historicity of the Colophonian account is disputed and archaeology indicates Greek settlement at the site earlier.
contested: The literary traditions are difficult to reconcile with one another and with the archaeology. The c. 660 BCE map stop is a traditional synchronization, not a securely observed year; evidence of Greek settlement may reach the late eighth or early seventh century BCE. The inherited Conquest and incorporation family classifies the structure described by the literary account; it is not independent confirmation that the takeover occurred exactly as narrated. The account does not reveal the number, removal, survival, incorporation, or property outcomes of Chonian residents.
displaced: Chonian inhabitants named in the literary account, whose presence and specific demographic outcome at the disputed foundation horizon are unresolved
settlers: Ionian refugees identified in later tradition with Colophon
Colonists who established or renamed the city Polieium
placeGloss: The line visualizes the Colophonian origin preserved in later ancient testimony. Strabo names Ionians but not Colophon, and neither source preserves an exact voyage; the origin and c. 660 BCE date are therefore marked as traditional.
evidence: Strabo 6.1.14 supplies the Ionian flight, Chonian predecessor city, forceful occupation, and Polieium name; the Oxford Inventory evaluates the conflicting traditions, Colophonian identification, c. 660 synchronization, and earlier archaeological chronology

name: Foundation of Himera and locally varied chora formation
mechanism: colonial foundation followed by locally varied land control, interaction, conflict, and political subjection
affectedLabel: Locally affected communities
actorLabel: Colonists / ruling polis
dates: 648 BCE traditional; archaeology supports mid-7th century BCE
story: Himera’s traditional foundation date is 648 BCE, and archaeological material is consistent with a mid-seventh-century beginning. Thucydides describes a foundation from Zancle by settlers mostly of Chalcidian descent, joined by Syracusan exiles. Archaeology in Himera’s territory shows no single uniform outcome: different places preserve settlement hierarchies, land-control systems, exchange and religious interaction, conflict, and military control.
contested: The 648 BCE date is traditional rather than exact, although it agrees broadly with the archaeological chronology. The territorial evidence varies by locality and cannot support a single removal rate, a uniform Indigenous response, or one dated frontier line. The atlas therefore treats Himera’s chora as one heterogeneous territorial formation rather than either a blanket displacement claim or unsupported micro-events.
displaced: Indigenous communities in Himera’s territory affected differently by settlement, land control, interaction, conflict, and military power
settlers: Settlers from Zancle, mostly of Chalcidian descent
Syracusan political exiles who joined the foundation
placeGloss: The two lines show the documented Zanclean foundation stream and the Syracusan exile contribution. They do not reconstruct individual voyages, and the destination marker does not imply that every Indigenous community in Himera’s wider territory experienced the same outcome.
evidence: Davies and Finglass synthesize the 648 BCE tradition, mid-seventh-century archaeology, Zanclean foundation, Chalcidian majority, and Syracusan exile contribution; Belvedere supplies locality-specific evidence for settlement hierarchy, land control, interaction, conflict, and military control

name: Achaean strategic resettlement of Metapontion
mechanism: strategic resettlement, rival territorial exclusion, war, and boundary settlement
affectedLabel: Territorially affected / contested
actorLabel: Inviting polis / settlers
dates: c. 630 BCE; later conflict chronology unresolved
story: Metapontion was founded around 630 BCE. In the tradition preserved by Strabo, Sybaris encouraged Achaean colonists to occupy the abandoned site so that Tarentines would not take it. The settlement was followed by war involving Tarentines and Oenotrians, then reconciliation and a defined territorial boundary. The event is therefore a strategic population placement and land-control program, not an empty-land migration.
contested: The foundation site is described as abandoned, but the wider land was claimed and contested. The sources do not date every phase, identify a continuous central administration, quantify the settlers, or show removal of a resident urban population. The c. 630 BCE stop dates the foundation; it does not collapse the later war and boundary settlement into the same year.
displaced: Oenotrian communities affected by the ensuing territorial conflict and boundary settlement
Tarentine claims excluded or constrained by the strategic resettlement
settlers: Achaean colonists encouraged to settle at Metapontion
Sybarite authorities associated in the tradition with the buffer-settlement decision
placeGloss: The route shows the Achaean settlement stream named in the literary tradition. It does not reconstruct a voyage, and the map does not treat the abandoned urban site as proof that the surrounding territory lacked Oenotrian use or competing Tarentine claims.
evidence: Carter supplies the modern c. 630 BCE foundation date; Strabo 6.1.15 supplies the abandoned-site resettlement, strategic exclusion of a Tarentine claim, subsequent war with Tarentines and Oenotrians, reconciliation, and boundary definition

name: Natives Land Act tenure prohibition and reserve dispossession
mechanism: racial land-tenure prohibition, anti-squatting rules, tenant displacement, labor subordination, eviction, and reserve confinement
affectedLabel: Dispossessed / confined / subordinated
actorLabel: State / landholders

internalSequence.label: Act No. 27 receives assent on 19 June and divides access to land through scheduled areas
Purchase and hire restrictions, anti-squatting enforcement, eviction, and reserve confinement continue without one defensible endpoint

story: The Natives Land Act of 1913 prohibited Black South Africans from purchasing or hiring land outside scheduled areas and restricted white acquisition within them. Its anti-squatting provisions attacked sharecropping and tenancy, encouraged landholders to replace Black tenants with servants or laborers, and exposed farm communities to eviction, loss of independent subsistence, and movement toward reserves.
contested: This was a national legal and property regime with locally uneven enforcement, not one synchronized relocation. The source does not provide a complete affected-household census, parcel-level dispossession map, or defensible terminal year. The map therefore shows statutory reach and regional context rather than an invented origin or removal route. The Conquest and incorporation family reflects the combined land-and-labor outcome; it does not deny physical eviction or reserve movement.
displaced: Black landholders, purchasers, tenants, sharecroppers, and farm communities barred from acquiring or hiring land outside scheduled areas
People exposed to tenant elimination, eviction, labor dependence, and movement toward reserves
settlers: The white-minority Union government and Parliament
White farmers and landowners applying the tenure and anti-squatting regime
placeGloss: The single point anchors a Union-wide legal regime on the map; it is not a removal destination. No route is drawn because the opened source does not provide one national movement path or one successor use for all dispossessed land.
evidence: South African History Online supplies the 19 June 1913 enactment, scheduled-area purchase and hire restrictions, anti-squatting provisions, tenant-to-laborer pressure, eviction, and reserve movement while leaving local counts, parcels, and the endpoint unresolved

name: Group Areas Act urban racial zoning and forced removals
mechanism: compulsory racial zoning, property and occupation restrictions, eviction, forced resettlement, demolition, and community destruction
affectedLabel: Removed / excluded
actorLabel: Apartheid authorities

cameraContext.name: Cape Town and the Cape Flats

internalSequence.label: The Group Areas Act establishes compulsory racial zoning and property restrictions
District Six is declared a white area; residents are removed toward the Cape Flats and most buildings are demolished
The Group Areas Act is repealed; dispossession and spatial segregation persist

story: The Group Areas Act of 1950 divided urban land into compulsory racial zones and restricted who could own, lease, occupy, or conduct business in them. State boards, police, local authorities, demolition, intimidation, and economic pressure removed Black, Coloured, and Indian communities from established neighborhoods. District Six to the Cape Flats is mapped as one documented example of a much wider national program.
contested: The mapped route does not exhaust the Group Areas program or imply that every removal followed the same timetable. Sophiatown is excluded because its removal used the separate Natives Resettlement Act, despite belonging to the same wider urban-apartheid project. The sources do not provide one municipality-by-municipality sequence, complete property ledger, household denominator, or remedy history. White occupation and redevelopment varied by locality, so the State-directed demographic remaking family does not assert one uniform settler-replacement stream.
displaced: Coloured, Indian, and African residents removed from District Six and other Cape Town communities toward the Cape Flats
Urban communities nationally subjected to racial zoning, property loss, eviction, and demolition
settlers: The National Party government, Parliament, the Group Areas Board, police, and state and local removal authorities
Property and redevelopment institutions that transferred or restricted occupation in proclaimed areas
placeGloss: The forced route is one bounded example: District Six residents were dispersed across the broad Cape Flats rather than to one precise point. It illustrates, but does not spatially total, the national Group Areas program.
evidence: South African History Online supports the 1950–1991 statutory frame and national coercive mechanism; its Cape Town history ties District Six to a Group Areas declaration and supplies the mapped origin, broad receiving geography, forced removal, and demolition sequence

name: Bantustan consolidation and community-removal program
mechanism: homeland tract consolidation, community-removal orders, black-spot clearance, forced resettlement, and boundary incorporation
affectedLabel: Removed / threatened / incorporated
actorLabel: Apartheid authorities

cameraContext.name: Transvaal black spots and homeland boundaries

internalSequence.label: Department planning and tract proposals provide the event’s documented evidence floor
The Black Laws Amendment Act extends removal-order power to a community as well as a tribe or part of one
Homeland consolidation intensifies through removals, black-spot clearance, and boundary changes
Resistance continues; some threatened removals are blocked while other communities are incorporated by redrawn boundaries

story: Apartheid authorities tried to consolidate fragmented Bantustans by purchasing and recombining tracts, removing communities and black spots, relocating townships toward homelands, and redrawing boundaries. Planning entries from 1972 and a 1973 amendment supply a documented evidence floor; the program intensified during the homeland-independence period. Physical removals, threatened removals, and territorial incorporation were related tools but not the same outcome.
contested: The 1972 date is an evidence floor, not proof that homeland engineering began that year, and the opened sources do not establish one endpoint. Proposals were not all executed: some communities resisted removal, while others were incorporated into a homeland by boundary changes without physically moving. The map therefore marks documented program regions but draws no route that would falsely convert every plan or boundary act into a completed relocation.
displaced: Black communities subjected to homeland-consolidation removal orders or forced relocation
Residents of black spots and townships targeted for clearance or movement toward a homeland
Communities threatened with removal or incorporated into a Bantustan through boundary changes
settlers: The apartheid government, Department of Bantu Development, Parliament, and officials planning consolidation and removal orders
Homeland administrations and state institutions involved in territorial consolidation
placeGloss: The points identify regions named in consolidation planning and later removal or boundary-incorporation evidence. They are not destinations and are not a complete homeland map; no movement route is drawn because the record includes proposals, resisted removals, completed removals, and boundary changes with different spatial meanings.
evidence: South African History Online supplies the 1972 planning floor, 1973 removal-order power, and Bantustan-removal category; the Truth and Reconciliation Commission documents the later consolidation drive, black-spot and township removals, community resistance, and the distinction between relocation and boundary incorporation

name: Cahokia-linked settlement and remaking of Aztalan
mechanism: incoming settlement, expansion and physical remaking of an occupied village, intermarriage, and cultural blending
affectedLabel: Prior residents / joined community
actorLabel: Cahokia-linked arrivals

internalSequence.label: Cahokia-linked visitors join an existing Late Woodland village around 1000
The village is expanded and remade around a plaza, platform mounds, and palisades
Middle Mississippian and Late Woodland people intermarry and their cultures blend
The village is abandoned for unknown reasons around 1200

story: A Late Woodland community already occupied the Crawfish River village when visitors linked to Cahokia arrived around 1000. The settlement was quickly expanded and remade with a central plaza, platform mounds, and palisades modeled on Cahokia. Over time Middle Mississippian and Late Woodland people intermarried and their cultures blended; the village was abandoned for unknown reasons around 1200.
contested: The sources do not establish conquest, forced entry, resident expulsion, or demographic replacement. The Wisconsin Historical Society synthesis notes cultural conflict and possible violent practices, but does not connect them to conquest, forced entry, or resident removal. Invitation, marriage, trade, or alliance remain possible, and the evidence does not provide population counts or land-tenure rules. The movement line shows a Cahokia-linked connection, not an exact surveyed route. Low-state durable expansion names the settlement and remaking of an occupied place without converting uncertainty into coercion.
displaced: Descendants of local Late Woodland Effigy Mound communities already living at the Crawfish River village
The later intermarried and culturally mixed Aztalan community; forced removal is not demonstrated
settlers: Visitors and settlers from Cahokia or with immediate ancestral ties to Cahokia
The pre-existing local village community participating in the later mixed settlement
placeGloss: Aztalan lies on the Crawfish River in present-day Wisconsin. The map begins at Cahokia near present-day St. Louis and ends at an already occupied village; it does not draw a local-removal route because none is documented.
evidence: Wisconsin Historical Society sections on the pre-existing Late Woodland village, Cahokia-linked arrival around 1000, rapid physical remaking, intermarriage and cultural blending, and abandonment for unknown reasons around 1200

name: Early Cahokian settlement and religious installation at Trempealeau
mechanism: intrusive Cahokian occupation, settlement, platform-mound and religious construction, and possible farmsteads
affectedLabel: Nearby local people / outcome unresolved
actorLabel: Cahokian settlers / builders

internalSequence.label: The bounded occupation begins immediately before 1050; no exact start year is known
Cahokian buildings, mounds, ceramics, imported tools, and possible farmsteads define the installation
The occupation ends before 1100; no exact terminal year is known

story: At the Trempealeau and Fisher Mounds complexes in western Wisconsin, Cahokian settlers built platform mounds, wall-trench structures, likely religious buildings, and possible farmsteads. Cahokian ceramics and imported stone tools mark a distinct occupation about 900 river kilometers north of Cahokia, beginning immediately before 1050 and ending before 1100.
contested: The peer-reviewed interpretation calls this an intrusive religious installation probably built by and for Cahokians with minimal involvement by living local people. It does not establish violence, forced removal, formal rule, land-tenure change, or the later fate of nearby communities. The exact start and end years, participant counts, and permanence of possible farmsteads remain unknown. Low-state durable expansion is the frozen model's nearest analytical family, not a claim that this less-than-century occupation was itself durable; the durability trait is zero. The family names the incoming installation, not demonstrated displacement.
displaced: Living local Upper Mississippi Valley people near the installation, whose identities and territorial outcomes are not named
No source-supported forced-removal population
settlers: Cahokian settlers and builders associated with the early occupation
Participants in the probable religious installation and possible farmsteads
placeGloss: Trempealeau lies on the Upper Mississippi in western Wisconsin. The line connects the source city and the installation for orientation; it is not an excavated travel itinerary and does not imply a local expulsion route.
evidence: Pauketat, Boszhardt, and Benden's peer-reviewed abstract supplies the bounded pre-1050 to pre-1100 chronology, Cahokian material signature, likely religious installation, and minimal local involvement; the Wisconsin Historical Society supplies regional context

name: Japanese railway-zone administration and urban settlement in southern Manchuria
mechanism: treaty-derived extraterritorial railway-land control, state-backed corporate administration, planned station-city construction, and Japanese urban migration
affectedLabel: Chinese residents / unequal colonial incorporation
actorLabel: Japanese state / South Manchuria Railway / urban migrants

internalSequence.label: Treaty rights give Japan control of the railway corridor and associated lands
The South Manchuria Railway Company is created and begins operating as a state-backed colonial institution
Railway-zone administration, planned station cities, and predominantly urban Japanese migration expand
The Manchurian Incident closes this bounded pre-Manchukuo phase

story: After the 1905 settlement of the Russo-Japanese War, Japan acquired treaty-based control of the southern Manchurian railway corridor and associated lands. The state-backed South Manchuria Railway Company directly administered the zone, built regulated station cities, and supplied transport, utilities, schools, hospitals, sanitation, real estate, mining, and experimental institutions. Japanese employees, merchants, professionals, and other migrants settled chiefly in these urban nodes before the 1931 Manchurian Incident transformed the colonial regime.
contested: The opened source establishes extraterritorial territorial control, planned colonial cities, and Japanese migration, but not a bounded Chinese removal campaign, a tract-specific displaced cohort, parcel-by-parcel ownership changes, complete resident counts, or event-specific lethal coercion. The map therefore shows colonial migration and railway-zone nodes, not an expulsion route. Conquest and incorporation is the frozen model's primary family: Chinese residents remained within an unequal colonial urban order, while their individual land and mobility outcomes remain unresolved.
displaced: Chinese residents and communities in and beside the railway municipalities, incorporated into an unequal colonial order
No source-bounded population can yet be labeled as forcibly removed by this specific 1905–1931 program
settlers: South Manchuria Railway administrators and employees
Japanese merchants, professionals, workers, and other predominantly urban migrants

targets.name: Dalian / Dairen railway and port zone

to.name: Dalian / Dairen railway and port zone

from.name: Dalian / Dairen railway and port zone

placeGloss: The map locates the Japanese source and two principal nodes of the southern Manchurian railway corridor. Its lines are migration and orientation links, not a claim that residents were deported along them.
evidence: Avila-Tàpies, printed pp. 38–45: treaty basis, railway lands, South Manchuria Railway administration, planned station cities, urban institutions, migration patterns, and the pre-/post-Manchukuo boundary

name: Japanese state and army agricultural colonization of Manchukuo
mechanism: army- and state-sponsored agricultural emigration, armed settler villages, forced or underpriced land transfer, collective-village removal, and Japanese occupation of vacated farms
affectedLabel: Chinese rural communities / displaced landholders and tenants
actorLabel: Japanese state / Kwantung Army / settler households

internalSequence.label: Army-backed trial emigration establishes armed agricultural settlements
The mass-migration campaign and million-household plan begin
Settler villages expand through strategic placement, coerced land transfer, and collective-village removal
Japan's defeat and the collapse of Manchukuo end the program

story: From 1932 the Kwantung Army and Japanese state institutions sponsored agricultural emigration to Manchukuo, first through armed trial settlements and from 1936 through a mass campaign. Planners placed settler villages along strategic border and transport corridors. Chinese farmers faced forced or underpriced land transfers; some rural communities were moved into collective villages, and Japanese settlers occupied vacated farms. The projected million-household scheme was never achieved and collapsed with Japan's defeat in 1945.
contested: The source directly supports state and army organization, coerced land transfer, collective-village removal, and settlement on vacated farms. It does not provide settlement-by-settlement chronology, complete settler or displaced-person totals, parcel histories, or a defensible regional fraction removed. The map marks the documented rural frontier and incoming settlement stream but does not invent precise removal destinations. State-directed demographic remaking is the frozen primary family because this program deliberately reorganized rural population and land; the rapid 1945 collapse is reflected in the low durability trait.
displaced: Chinese peasants, landholders, tenants, and rural communities whose farms, homes, or villages were taken or reorganized
People moved into controlled collective villages; complete numbers and destinations remain unresolved
settlers: Japanese agricultural settler households and armed emigrants
Youth Brigade members and settlers organized by army, state, and colonial-development institutions
placeGloss: The map connects Japan to Jiamusi, a documented arrival and staging point, and to a broader northern settlement-frontier marker. Jiamusi is not presented as the settlers' final agricultural site. Documented land clearance occurred within the wider northern zone, but no source-bounded destination supports drawing a precise forced-removal arrow.
evidence: McDowell: trial emigration from 1932, mass migration from 1936, army and state organization, forced or underpriced land transfers, collective-village removal, settlement on vacated farms, strategic village placement, and collapse in 1945

name: Latin colonial reconstitution of Ariminum
mechanism: state-directed Latin colonial reconstitution of an existing settlement on conquered Ager Gallicus
affectedLabel: Umbrian or Gallic residents / landholders
actorLabel: Roman Republic / Latin colonists
story: An existing Umbrian and Gallic settlement in conquered Ager Gallicus was reconstituted as a Latin colony.
contested: No source establishes complete resident removal, settler or resident totals, or parcel-level succession at Ariminum. Confidence: high on the 268 BCE Latin colony, the existing settlement, conquered regional land, and durable colonial reconstitution; low on settler totals, parcel division, household composition, resident legal shares, movement, and population proportions.
displaced: Umbrian or Gallic residents and landholders affected by Ariminum's colonial reconstitution
settlers: Roman Republic
Latin colonists at Ariminum
placeGloss: Ariminum is present-day Rimini. The line shows the incoming colonial connection from Rome, not a resident-removal route; continued local residence is documented more clearly than any expulsion.
evidence: Oxford and Papers of the British School at Rome treatments of the 268 BCE Latin colony, the pre-existing settlement, and its Ager Gallicus setting

name: Senone expulsion and Roman colony at Sena Gallica
mechanism: conquest, killing and expulsion of Senone residents, followed by a Roman colony on their territory
affectedLabel: Senone communities / expelled survivors
actorLabel: Roman Republic / colonists at Sena Gallica

internalSequence.label: Roman victory, killing, and expulsion remove Senone survivors from the territory
The Roman colony at Sena Gallica establishes a successor settlement; the exact year remains disputed

story: Senone survivors expelled from their territory and a Roman colony planted at Sena Gallica.
contested: The expelled population's destination and count are unknown; Polybius's totalizing phrase is not a census; modern chronology varies between 284 and 283 BCE. Confidence: high on the bounded killing-expulsion-colony sequence; medium on chronology and land scope; low on population totals, destinations, household composition, and survivor demography.
displaced: Senone communities in Ager Gallicus
settlers: Roman Republic
Roman army and citizen colonists at Sena Gallica
placeGloss: Sena Gallica is shown on the northern Adriatic. The incoming line marks Roman colonization; no outward expulsion arrow is drawn because neither the Senones' destination nor their number is known.
evidence: Polybius 2.19 for the expulsion and territorial outcome; modern chronology and regional cross-check in the Journal of Roman Studies

name: Forced lowland transfer of the Ligurian Friniates
mechanism: state-compelled disarmament and internal relocation from mountain country to an assigned plain
affectedLabel: Ligurian Friniates and related groups
actorLabel: Roman Republic / Marcus Aemilius
story: Friniates and other Ligurian groups disarmed and transferred from hills to plains by Marcus Aemilius.
contested: Livy supplies neither a count nor a precise destination and does not identify an incoming population. Confidence: high on a bounded compelled hill-to-plain relocation; medium on its security purpose; low on population share, precise destinations, household composition, tenure, return, and later status.
displaced: Ligurian Friniates and other Ligurian communities moved from hills to plains
settlers: Roman Republic
Marcus Aemilius and the Roman army

targets.name: Assigned lowland area — precise site unknown

to.name: Assigned lowland area — precise site unknown

evidence: Livy 39 and the Journal of Roman Studies cross-check for disarmament and compulsory hill-to-plain transfer; no incoming population is identified

name: Quintus Fulvius's forced Ligurian lowland concentration
mechanism: state-compelled movement to the plains combined with military occupation of the source mountains
affectedLabel: Residents of an unnamed Ligurian district
actorLabel: Roman Republic / Quintus Fulvius
story: After surrender Quintus Fulvius brought the district's Ligurian population into the plains and garrisoned the mountains.
contested: The subgroup, precise source district, precise destination, and whether Livy's 3,200 denotes fighters or all surrendering residents are unresolved; modern dates vary between 180 and 179 BCE. Confidence: high on a separate compelled lowland concentration; medium on chronology; low on subgroup identity, source district, destination, population share, count, household composition, and later status.
displaced: Residents of an unnamed Ligurian district compelled into the plains
settlers: Roman Republic
Quintus Fulvius and the Roman army

targets.name: Assigned Ligurian lowland area — precise site unknown

to.name: Assigned Ligurian lowland area — precise site unknown

placeGloss: The subgroup, source district, and destination are unresolved. The map uses approximate Ligurian highland and lowland markers and does not equate this operation with the separately documented Apuan transfer to Samnium.
evidence: Livy 40 and the Journal of Roman Studies cross-check for surrender, compulsory lowland concentration, and garrisoning of the mountain source area

name: Twin Latin colonies at Cremona and Placentia
mechanism: linked frontier colonies on Gallic land, immediate armed resistance, and later family reinforcement
affectedLabel: Boii and Insubres / local landholders
actorLabel: Roman Republic / Latin colonists

internalSequence.label: One commission founds Cremona and Placentia with about 6,000 colonists reported at each
Gallic resistance immediately threatens the two colonies
A reported reinforcement of 6,000 families sustains the linked project

story: Rome founded Cremona and Placentia together on Gallic land with about six thousand colonists at each site; Gallic resistance followed and a later six-thousand-family reinforcement sustained the two colonies.
contested: The evidence does not assign each affected resident or parcel to Boii versus Insubres, prove total removal, or support treating the 190 reinforcement as a fresh land-taking event. Confidence: high on the simultaneous 218 BCE foundations, attributed six-thousand-person stream at each site, Gallic resistance, and later joint six-thousand-family reinforcement; low on Boii-versus-Insubres parcel assignment, resident movement, removal share, casualty proportions, initial household composition, and prior ancestry in the successor communities.
displaced: Boii and Insubres communities and landholders affected by the two colonial territories
settlers: Roman Republic
Latin colonists and later reinforcing families at Cremona and Placentia
placeGloss: The two cities are one statistical event because one commission founded them together and the later reinforcement sustained the same linked project. The lines show incoming settlement, not two separate events or resident-removal routes.
evidence: Polybius 3, Livy 21.25 and book 37, plus the Placentia archaeological record for the linked foundations, resistance, and reinforcement

name: Boii land confiscation and the Latin colony at Bononia
mechanism: postwar confiscation of nearly half the Boii territory and ranked allotments to a Latin colony
affectedLabel: Boii communities / landholders
actorLabel: Roman Republic / Latin colonists

internalSequence.label: After Boii surrender, Rome takes nearly half their territory
Bononia is founded with 3,000 Latin colonists and ranked allotments

story: After Boii surrender Rome took nearly half their territory and founded Bononia with three thousand Latin colonists and ranked land allotments.
contested: The battle totals are source claims rather than census data; neither the half-territory clause nor the foundation notice proves that all Boii residents were expelled from the colonial allotments. Confidence: high on Boii surrender, the attributed near-half territorial taking, the 3,000-person colony, and ranked allotments; low on resident movement, affected-household share, casualty proportions, household composition, local continuity, and prior ancestry in the successor community.
displaced: Boii communities and landholders affected by territorial confiscation and colonial allotment
settlers: Roman Republic
Latin colonists at Bononia
placeGloss: Bononia is present-day Bologna. The map shows the incoming colonial connection; it does not turn the nearly-half-territory clause into a claim that all Boii residents were expelled.
evidence: Livy books 36–37 and the Bononia archaeological record for surrender, confiscation, the 3,000-colonist report, and ranked allotments

name: Twin citizen colonies at Mutina and Parma
mechanism: one commission founding two citizen colonies with individual allotments on former Boii territory
affectedLabel: Boii communities / rural prior holders unknown
actorLabel: Roman Republic / citizen colonists
story: One commission founded the twin citizen colonies of Mutina and Parma in former Boii territory with two thousand colonists at each and different allotment sizes.
contested: Mutina had a pre-colonial fortified settlement while Parma's city site lacks secure immediate prehistory; neither condition identifies every prior rural landholder or proves total resident removal. Confidence: high on the single 183 BCE commission, two linked sites, attributed two-thousand-person stream at each, former Boii source land, and ranked allotments; low on immediate rural holders, resident movement, household composition, local population shares, and whether later residents represent continuity, return, or migration.
displaced: Boii and other prior landholders affected by the Mutina and Parma colonial tracts
settlers: Roman Republic
Roman citizen colonists at Mutina and Parma
placeGloss: Mutina and Parma are one event because one 183 BCE commission founded both. Separate lines mark the two sites without claiming total Boii removal or turning each city into a second statistical row.

name: Removal of Transalpine Gauls and the colony at Aquileia
mechanism: forced evacuation of a recent Gallic settlement and successor Latin colonization of the frontier region
affectedLabel: Recent Transalpine Gallic settlers
actorLabel: Roman Republic / Latin colonists

affectedLabel: Scionaean community, including killed adult men and enslaved women and children
actorLabel: Athens as coercive authority; Plataeans as successor inhabitants
story: Thucydides reports that after Athens reduced Scione in 421 BCE, it killed the adult men, enslaved the women and children, and gave the land to Plataeans to inhabit. The Plataean tenure ended with a separate Scionaean restoration conventionally dated to 405 BCE.
contested: The 406 endpoint is analytical—the last full year before the separate restoration—not a new action in 406. Captive destinations, casualty and captive totals, survivor outcomes, the immediate origin and number of Plataean inhabitants, households, parcels, labor arrangements, and the restored cohort are unknown.

Scionaean women and children reported enslaved, without destinations or totals
Other survivors and later returnees whose number, location, and route are unknown
settlers: Athens as the directing and attacking authority
Plataeans given the land to inhabit, without a supported immediate-origin route or population profile

evidence: Thucydides 5.32.1 for the 421 destruction, enslavement, and land grant; Plutarch, Lysander 14.3, for the separately bounded restoration; ToposText for the representative site

name: Labici's capture, plunder, and colonial land allotment

story: Livy reports that Roman forces captured and plundered Labici in 418 BCE. He then reports a Senate-ordered settlement of 1,500 colonists, each receiving two iugera on the conquered Labican land.
contested: The account is retrospective and the figures are Livy's report. The city's exact site and the settlement's legal form are disputed; 1,500 may be Rome's share or the whole body including allies. Resident displacement, casualties, prior parcels, complete households, individual origins, labor relations, and the settler body's later continuity are unknown.

story: Livy reports that five commissioners were appointed in 383 BCE to divide Pomptine land. In 358 BCE he records the creation of the Pomptina tribe. name: Roman destruction of Carthage, captive removal, and territorial annexation

story: After a three-year siege, Roman forces took Carthage in a six-day urban assault marked by fire, collapsing buildings, and extensive killing. contested: Appian's 50,000 is a transmitted ancient claim, not a census, and his opened account does not say that this group was sold. Orosius, writing much later, separately gives 25,000 women and 30,000 men and says nearly all captives were sold. The two totals describe different accounts and are not combined. No exact death total, captive destination register, complete survivor denominator, or evidence for sowing the site with salt is available.

name: Sullan proscriptions: killing, banishment, and confiscated estates
mechanism: public proscription lists; licensed and rewarded killing; penalties for concealment; banishment and flight; state confiscation and sale or transfer of houses and estates; civic disability imposed on descendants
affectedLabel: Named political targets, their households and helpers, heirs and descendants, and owners of confiscated houses and estates across Rome and Roman Italy; totals and local population shares unknown

dates: 82–81 BCE; 1 June 81 is the best-attested legal cutoff, not a universal end
story: After Sulla's victory in 82 BCE, his regime published lists that stripped named opponents of legal protection. Killers and informers could be rewarded, concealment was penalized, and targeted people were killed, banished, or driven into flight. Houses and estates could be confiscated and sold or transferred, while civic disabilities extended to descendants.
contested: The ancient authors agree on the system but give incompatible list totals and sweeping descriptions that are not a death census or complete map of affected people and property. Cicero makes 1 June 81 BCE the best-attested legal cutoff, yet his Roscius case also alleges abuse after it; killing, pursuit, litigation, sales, exile, and disability did not all end on one demonstrated day. Ameria illustrates how dispossession could operate, but it is not representative of every estate. Community punishments and veteran colonies are separate local events, not parts of this national statistical unit.

story: After Volaterrae's surrender around 79 BCE, a Sullan measure deprived the community of civic rights and made its land Roman public land. Yet the intended division was not completed. Citizenship deprivation did not durably succeed, and practical possession continued. Santangelo reads the distribution as unexecuted; Thein allows that limited individual allotments may have occurred. The c. 79 BCE stop marks the surrender and operative penalty, while disputes in 63, 60, 59, and 46/45 BCE are the measure's afterlife, not one continuous event.
